Getting Started
Overview

whip framework

What whip is

whip is a complete base for a FiveM server. Install it on an empty server and your players can make a character, carry and stash things, keep money in the bank, buy, fuel and tune a car, own a home and furnish it, and be hurt and revived. You run the server from inside the game: /whip opens an admin panel for players, items, settings, banks, garages, shops and homes, so most changes need no code. whip needs only FiveM and oxmysql. It does not use QBCore, ESX or ox_core, and it replaces the inventory, target, garage and banking resources they rely on.

It is written for two kinds of people. Server owners install it, change its settings in game, and build the world (garages, shops, homes, doors, zones) without opening a file. Developers write resources on top of it: a job, a shop, a mission. whip already does what every resource needs (saving, checking what players' games send, the screens and prompts), so the code you write is mostly the part that is new.

What makes it different:

  • Safe by default. A modified game can send your server anything. With SecureEvent you write, beside your handler, what it accepts: how often, which values, how close the player must stand. whip turns everything else away before your code runs.
  • Items are real things. Cash is banknotes in a pocket, so it can be dropped, stolen or put in a safe. A bag weighs what is in it, and a car's boot holds things just like a stash does.
  • Nothing is half saved. Everything one action changes (the money taken, the item given) is saved together, so a crash never leaves a player charged for something they didn't get.
  • Settings live in the game. The settings an owner changes are in /whip → Settings, checked as you type, and your own resource can add a page of its own beside them.

Where to start

  • You run a server: Quick Start installs whip and checks it works. After that, Server Owners covers the settings, the admin tools and building in game.
  • You want to build on whip: Your First Resource takes you from an empty folder to a working coffee stand in about thirty minutes. Read How whip thinks alongside it.
  • You know QBCore or ESX: Coming from QBCore, ESX or ox says what to keep, what to remove, and which whip call replaces each one you know.

What's in WHIP

WHIP is whip_core and the resources built on it. Each of them needs only whip_core, so you can leave out any you don't want.

ResourceKindPurpose
whip_coreCorePlayers, characters, inventory, money and banks, jobs, vehicles, garages, properties, prompts, the UI library, the Director, the admin panel and developer tools
whip_gunnyFeatureWeapons: magazine-fed and magless guns, calibers, melee, throwables, attachments at the weapon bench
whip_fuelFeatureA fuel tank on every car, petrol pumps with a hose, the jerry can
whip_ropeFeatureA physics rope: carry it, tie it, tow with it
whip_phoneFeatureThe Duo phone: a phone shell whose apps are modules, from whip or any resource
whip_autos, whip_autos_shopFeatureWhiplash: a customisation shop, turbos and nitrous; the shop building in Burton
whip_voiceFeatureVoice chat on your own voice server, placed in 3D
whip_chat, whip_loadingscreenFeaturewhip's chat and loading screen
whip_media_clothing_male, whip_media_clothing_female, whip_media_props, whip_media_previews, whip_media_mapMediaClothing, furniture, vehicle, NPC and tattoo pictures, emote videos and the map, kept out of whip_core so its updates stay small. They are in [assets]/[media]; the two map packs are in [assets]
whip_homes_mirrorparkMapEvery Mirror Park house as a walk-in home with its own interior, and 25 walk-in garages
whip_graphicsMapLED streetlights and whip's look for the city's light and sky

The same resources run on both games. Each map pack carries its models twice, stream/ for Legacy and stream_enhanced/ for GTA V Enhanced, and an Enhanced server says which it is with one line in server.cfg (below).

How the pieces fit together, for developers: How whip is built.

Quick Start

From nothing to your first character in game. whip is installed as a new server, by txAdmin: its recipe makes the whole server (the resources, the database and server.cfg). It is not added to a server you already have. Each step says only what to do; Running whip, under Server Owners, explains what happens behind it and what to do when a step goes wrong.

1. What you need

  • FiveM's server with txAdmin: Legacy (the FXServer server, artifact 38435 or newer) or Enhanced (the cfx-server server). WHIP runs on both.
  • MariaDB 10.2.3 or newer, or MySQL 8.0.16 or newer, and a login that may create a database.
  • About 1 GB of disk, and at least 10 Mbit/s to GitHub. txAdmin gives each download 150 seconds, and the largest of whip's is about 145 MB.
  • The voice ports open inbound, as for 30120: UDP 7882-7893 and TCP 7881. whip_voice runs its own voice server on this machine (Setting up whip_voice).

2. Install whip

  1. Start the server and open txAdmin. On its setup page choose Remote URL Template and paste the recipe for your game:
# Legacy
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WHIPFX/txAdmin-recipe/main/whip-legacy.yaml

# Enhanced
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WHIPFX/txAdmin-recipe/main/whip-enhanced.yaml
  1. Give it your server key (from portal.cfx.re) and your database login. txAdmin downloads each WHIP resource at its release, and WHIPFX's build of oxmysql; makes an empty database (WHIP builds every table it needs the first time it starts, and no WHIP resource has an SQL file to import); turns OneSync on; writes server.cfg; and makes your txAdmin account an admin. WHIP's ten resources land at the top of resources, the media and map packs in [assets], and oxmysql in [ox].
  2. Start the server.

The server.cfg it writes

sv_licenseKey "your key"
set mysql_connection_string "mysql://user:password@localhost/whip_1A2B3C"

# Legacy only: the game build whip's car, prop and clothing lists are made for (or newer)
sv_enforceGameBuild 3407

# Players need a Steam account linked to their Cfx.re account
set sv_enforceSteamAuth true

ensure oxmysql
ensure whip_core
ensure whip_autos
ensure whip_autos_shop
ensure whip_chat
ensure whip_fuel
ensure whip_gunny
ensure whip_loadingscreen
ensure whip_phone
ensure whip_rope
# whip_voice runs its own voice server on this machine: FXServer lets a resource start a program only with this line
add_unsafe_child_process_permission whip_voice
ensure whip_voice
ensure [assets]    # the media packs and the map packs

# The admin tools (/w and /whip) for everyone in group.admin, which your txAdmin account is in
add_ace group.admin whip.devtools allow
add_principal identifier.fivem:1234567 group.admin

The order of WHIP's ensure lines doesn't matter; only oxmysql has to come before them. Your own resources go after them. FiveM's own chat, spawnmanager and basic-gamemode are not installed: whip has its own.

On an Enhanced server (the cfx-server server) the recipe writes two other lines in place of sv_enforceGameBuild:

setr whip_platform enhanced
set sv_resourceFileDownloadTimeout 600000

The first tells whip, and the map packs' scripts, that it is on Enhanced. It must be setr, not set, so that players' games get it too. The second gives a player on a slow connection long enough to download the media packs.

3. Check it works

  1. Start the server. A few seconds after Framework loaded successfully!, the console prints a whip setup block: what whip found, and a line marked FIX for anything you need to change, with the line that fixes it. Type whipsetup in the server console to see it again.
  2. Join the server. Your Cfx.re account needs a Steam account linked to it: the recipe turns on sv_enforceSteamAuth, and FiveM asks players who have none to link one. You should see the character screen. Make a character, and the appearance creator opens.
  3. You are an admin already: the recipe put your txAdmin account in group.admin. For another admin, they type /w, and the server console prints their add_ace line. Type it into the console (it works at once), and put it in server.cfg to keep it.
  4. In game, F2 opens the inventory and Tab shows the hotbar. /w has the quick tools (noclip, coordinates) and /whip opens the admin panel.

Updating

Each whip resource is released on its own, on its GitHub page. Read whip_core/CHANGELOG.md first. Then stop the server and replace the resource's folder with the new release's (Source code (zip) on its releases page). The database is left as it is: whip_core changes its tables to match on the next start.

What the server wrote into the old folder is yours to carry over: the Director packs you exported (whip_core/pack_exports), pictures taken in game (img/props in whip_media_props, img/vehicles in whip_media_previews) and the engine list from /whiplashengines (whip_autos/engines.json).

Next: Server Owners for the settings and admin tools, or Your First Resource to build something.

How whip thinks

Five ideas, and everything else in these docs follows from them.

1. A player, a character, a session

account        userId     made the first time they connect; staff permissions belong here
 └ character   charId     up to Config.MaxCharacters per account; kept for ever: save this one
    └ loaded on a server id (source), for one session (player.session), until logout
IdNamesLastsTaken by
sourceA connected playerUntil they leave. The next player can get the same numberEverything about someone online: GetPlayer, AddItem, NotifyPlayer
{ charId = n }A character, online or notFor everCalls that can reach someone offline: PayPlayer, GiveOnLogin, the bank. Such a call takes a person: a source or { charId = n }
userIdAn accountFor everStaff permissions (GrantPermission)
player.sessionOne load of a characterUntil logoutIsSessionCurrent, after your handler waited
vehicleIdA car whip knowsOwned: for ever. Any other: until the restartEvery vehicle export (Vehicle references)

2. Every place items sit is a store

Pockets, a stash, a car's boot, glovebox and ignition, a shop, a wallet: each is a store, named by one shape, { kind, id, sub, slot }. One engine moves items between any two (StoreMove), with the same checks, so a resource that can move an item into a stash can move one into a boot.

3. Memory is the truth, the database catches up

whip changes its own memory at once and writes what changed within about a second. Everything one player action changes (a SecureEvent handler, a use handler) is written in one transaction, so a crash never leaves half of it. Your own tables are yours: call SavePlayer between an inventory change and your own write (Save System).

4. What you declare lives in whip_core's memory

Items, use handlers, actions, secure events: whip_core keeps them in memory and forgets them when it restarts. So they go in Whip.register, which declares them again (the one rule).

5. The server decides

A player's game only asks. A SecureEvent checks who asked, how often, from where, and every value, before your handler runs; your handler decides. What a client is shown (an action's require) is a courtesy, never the check.

Where your data lives

Your dataPut it inWho saves itWho sees it
Items and cash a player carriesTheir pockets: AddItem, PayPlayerwhip, with the actionThe player; admins
Something about one item: a serial, rounds, wearIts metadata: SetItemMetadatawhip, with the itemThe holder's game too: never a secret
A fact about a character: a licence, quest progressA flag: SetPlayerFlag, or SetPlayerMetadata. Both while the character is on; for someone offline, GiveOnLogin or the bankwhip, with the characterTheir own game too: never a secret
Something about a car: a fitted part, a finance flagSetVehicleData; a gauge (fuel, boost) is a vehicle statwhip, with the carGames near the car, for a stat
Items kept somewhere new: a mailbox, a vaultA container (EnsureContainer), or a store kind of your ownwhip, like every storeWhoever its rules let open it
Your resource's settingsA settings page: Whip.configPage or RegisterSettingswhip, in the databaseAdmins change it in /whip (Settings pages); every game reads it, unless the setting says sides = 'server'
A player's own choice: a volume, a toggleWhip.playerSettingTheir own PCThat player (Each player's own settings)
Anything else: a ledger, a leaderboardA table of your own (oxmysql), made with EnsureTableYou. Write it with CommitWithAction when it follows an inventory changeWhoever your code shows it to
An item for a character who is awayGiveOnLoginwhip, in the database, until their next loginThem, when it arrives
EnsureTable(name, createSql, migrations?)SERVER

A table of your own, built the way whip builds its own, so a buyer never imports a .sql file. createSql is one CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS with the table complete: it makes the table on a database without it and does nothing on one that has it. Its text sorts by utf8mb4_unicode_ci, as whip's own tables do, unless createSql names a COLLATE of its own. migrations are the changes you make after release, in order and only ever added to: each runs once per database (recorded as '<your resource>:<id>'). When this call makes the table, its CREATE already has every change, so the migrations are recorded as done without running. On a table made before a change, each statement says what it is about and is skipped when it is there. Put the change in both: the CREATE for a new server, a migration for one that already has the table.

Whip.register(function()
    local ok, why = exports.whip_core:EnsureTable('mycafe_orders', [[
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS `mycafe_orders` (
            `id`     INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
            `charId` INT          NOT NULL,
            `note`   VARCHAR(200) NULL,
            PRIMARY KEY (`id`)
        ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4]], {
        { id = '002_note', statements = {
            { sql = 'ALTER TABLE `mycafe_orders` ADD COLUMN `note` VARCHAR(200) NULL',
              unless = { column = { 'mycafe_orders', 'note' } } },
        } },
    })
    if not ok then print('mycafe: ' .. why) end
end)
Returns: true, or false, why: a bad name or statement, or the first migration that failed (the ones after it wait for the next start). Write rows that follow an inventory change with CommitWithAction, below. A guard is unless or onlyIf with { column = { table, name } }, { index = … } or { constraint = … }; a migration may give a run function instead, that looks first and answers false to be tried again next start
CommitWithAction(queries, opts?)SERVER

Your own queries in one transaction with everything the player's current action has changed and whip has not yet written: the item you took and the ledger row you wrote for it land together, or neither does. Outside an action, the queries alone. Call it from the handler (a SecureEvent, a use handler) that made the change; from elsewhere, say whose action with opts.source (and opts.vehicleId).

local ok, why = exports.whip_core:RemoveItem(source, 'mycafe_coffee', 1)
if not ok then return false, why end
ok, why = exports.whip_core:CommitWithAction({
    { query = 'INSERT INTO `mycafe_orders` (`charId`, `note`) VALUES (?, ?)', values = { player.charId, 'coffee' } },
})
Returns: true, or false, why (the database refused it: nothing of the transaction landed, and whip writes its own part again later)
GiveOnLogin(who, item, amount?, metadata?, reason?)SERVER

An item for someone who may not be playing: a prize for an offline winner, a refund owed, something taken back while they were away. Playing now, they get it now, as AddItem. Away, it is kept in the database and handed over at their next login, into their pockets or at their feet when full, logged with your reason. who: a server id or { charId = n }.

exports.whip_core:GiveOnLogin({ charId = winner }, 'mycafe_voucher', 1, nil, 'raffle prize')
Returns: 'now' or 'login', or false, why (an unknown item, a bad amount, nobody by that charId)

Your First Resource

About thirty minutes from an empty folder to a coffee stand: a counter you walk up to, a purchase the server checks and charges for, and a coffee that takes four seconds to drink. Each step is something every whip resource does.

StepWhat you learn
1. The folderThe manifest lines every whip resource has
2. Where the counter isFinding a position in game
3. The itemWhip.register: the one rule
4. Drinking itA timed use the server runs
5. Selling itSecureEvent, near, a receipt and a refund
6. The counterA prompt, with AddAction
7. Try itTesting, and watching the calls in the Monitor

You need a server running whip_core (Quick Start), and the whip.devtools ACE for yourself so /w and /whip open: one add_ace line in server.cfg, shown in Quick Start step 3.

The finished stand is in whip_core/docs/examples/whip_cafe_example: this page and Your First Job, line for line, with the coffee's picture. Compare yours with it when a step will not work. It never starts by itself; to run it, copy the folder into your resources folder and ensure it. It uses the same names as yours, so run one of the two.

1. The folder

Make a folder called mycafe in your resources, holding four files: fxmanifest.lua, shared.lua, server.lua and client.lua. The manifest:

fx_version 'cerulean'
game 'gta5'
lua54 'yes'

dependency 'whip_core'

shared_scripts {
    '@whip_core/lib/satellite.lua',   -- whip's helper: gives you Whip.register
    'shared.lua',
}
server_script 'server.lua'
client_script 'client.lua'

dependency 'whip_core' makes the server start whip_core first. @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua is whip's helper file, and step 3 is about what it gives you. Add ensure mycafe to server.cfg, below WHIP's ensure lines.

Your editor, before you write a line. Copy whip_core/types/luarc.template.json into mycafe as .luarc.json and open the folder in VS Code with the Lua extension (by sumneko). Every exports.whip_core:… call and every Whip.* then shows its parameters and what it answers, and a misspelt name is underlined. It finds WHIP's types whether mycafe sits next to whip_core (as here) or next to a [whip] folder that holds it. For FiveM's own functions (GetEntityCoords and the rest), add a natives extension such as CfxLua IntelliSense. One thing the editor cannot do is tell a server file from a client one: it offers both sides' calls everywhere. Hover a call to see its side (WhipCoreServerExports or WhipCoreClientExports), or read the SERVER / CLIENT mark on its card.

With the dependency, your resource also stops when whip_core stops, and whip_core starts it again once it is back up (the console says so). So a whip_core restart is a fresh start for your resource too. A resource you stopped by hand stays stopped.

2. Where the counter is

Both sides need the counter's position: the client to put the prompt there, and the server to refuse a purchase from anyone standing somewhere else. So it goes in shared.lua:

-- Read by both sides: the client puts the prompt here, and the server refuses
-- a purchase from anyone who is not standing here.
Config = {
    Counter = vector3(-361.0, 49.0, 54.4),   -- a step in front of where new characters spawn
    Price   = 15,
}

That spot is just in front of where a new character appears, so you can test straight away. For your own spot, stand there in game, open /w → Coords and press G: it copies vector4(x, y, z, heading) to your clipboard. The first three numbers go in the vector3.

3. The item, and the one rule

Everything whip_core owns (the item registry, use handlers, events, interaction points) lives in memory. When whip_core restarts it forgets your item: no weight, no label, no use. So everything you declare to whip goes in one function whip can run again, handed to Whip.register. In server.lua:

-- server.lua
Whip.register(function()
    exports.whip_core:RegisterItem('mycafe_coffee', {
        name     = 'Coffee',
        desc     = 'Hot and black. Quenches thirst.',
        weight   = 0.3,
        type     = 'consumable',
        stack    = true,
        maxStack = 10,
        usable   = true,
    })
end)

Your function runs once whip_core is ready, whichever of you started first, and again after every whip_core restart (with the dependency that is your resource's own fresh start, step 1). It does not run again when some unrelated resource starts. Every field an item can have is under Item Definition.

Running it twice is safe. Every whip registration follows one rule: registering the same thing again changes nothing, and registering something different under your own name replaces it. You never need a "did I already register this?" flag.
Don't wait a fixed time and hope whip_core is up. CreateThread(function() Wait(1000) … end) is a guess at a load order nobody controls, and it registers once, so a whip_core restart silently strips everything your resource declared. Watching onResourceStart for 'whip_core' has the same problem the other way round: it misses the first start.

The helper also gives you Whip.call('ExportName', …), which answers false, reason instead of erroring while whip_core is down, Whip.onCoreLost(fn) and Whip.ready(timeoutMs). See The satellite helper.

4. Drinking it

Below RegisterItem, inside the same function, say what using the coffee does. Handing RegisterUseHandler a table instead of a function makes it a timed use: whip shows the bar, plays the animation, puts the cup in their hand, and times the bar on the server, so a modified client cannot skip it. When the bar ends, whip takes the coffee and then runs onComplete.

    -- Drinking it: a 4-second bar, a cup in the right hand, and they can walk meanwhile
    exports.whip_core:RegisterUseHandler('mycafe_coffee', {
        label    = 'Drinking coffee...',
        duration = 4000,
        anim     = { dict = 'amb@world_human_drinking@coffee@male@idle_a', clip = 'idle_c' },
        prop     = { model = 'p_amb_coffeecup_01', bone = 28422 },
        disable  = { move = false },

        -- The bar finished and the coffee is gone. Return AddStat's answer:
        -- if it fails, whip gives the coffee back.
        onComplete = function(source)
            return exports.whip_core:AddStat(source, 'thirst', 20, 'item:mycafe_coffee')
        end,
    })

whip's thirst runs from 100 (full) down to 0. A new character starts full, so the drink only shows on the gauge once thirst has drained a little (Stats & Effects). AddStat answers true, or false, why; returning that answer means a drink that failed costs the player nothing. Every field is on the RegisterUseHandler card.

Try it now. In the server console, refresh then ensure mycafe; from now on, restart mycafe after each change. In game, open /whip → Economy → Items, search for coffee and give yourself one. Press F2, right-click the coffee and choose Use.

5. Selling it

Still inside the same function: the purchase. A SecureEvent is RegisterNetEvent with the checks built in, and each line here closes a way to cheat.

    -- Buying one. The client sends nothing: not the price, not the item.
    exports.whip_core:SecureEvent('mycafe:buy', {
        rateLimit = 1000,   -- one purchase a second per player
        near = { at = Config.Counter, range = 3.0, message = 'Walk up to the counter' },
    }, function(source)
        local receipt, err = exports.whip_core:ChargePlayer(source, Config.Price, { reason = 'Coffee' })
        if not receipt then
            return false, err   -- could not pay: whip shows them why
        end

        local given, why = exports.whip_core:AddItem(source, 'mycafe_coffee', 1)
        if not given then
            exports.whip_core:RefundPlayer(receipt)   -- paid, got nothing: money back
            return false, why
        end

        exports.whip_core:NotifyPlayer(source, 'Enjoy your coffee', 'success')
    end)
  • The client sends nothing. The price and the item are the server's. A client that could send the price could send 0.
  • near refuses anyone more than 3 m from the counter before your function runs, and shows them your message. Without it, a modified client could buy from anywhere on the map.
  • rateLimit allows one call a second per player. Extra calls are refused and logged.
  • ChargePlayer takes cash if they carry enough, otherwise the bank, and answers a receipt, or false and a sentence the player can read. See Charging a Player.
  • RefundPlayer gives the money back when the coffee could not be given. AddItem normally drops what does not fit at the player's feet, but a server can turn that off, so check its answer.
  • return false, why refuses: the player is shown why, and the refusal is recorded.
  • Exports called straight. Inside a handler whip_core runs (a SecureEvent, a SecureCallback, a use handler), whip_core is up, and the payment and the coffee are written together. In code of your own (a thread, a command, a timer, an NUI callback), call through Whip.core:ChargePlayer(...) instead: the same call, which answers false, why when whip_core is not running instead of throwing (Calling whip_core).

6. The counter

In client.lua, put a prompt at the counter. Walk up and it appears; press E and it sends the event:

-- client.lua
Whip.register(function()
    exports.whip_core:AddAction({
        id       = 'counter',
        at       = { coords = Config.Counter },
        label    = ('Buy coffee ($%d)'):format(Config.Price),
        icon     = 'cash',
        onSelect = function()
            TriggerServerEvent('mycafe:buy')
        end,
    })
end)

AddAction goes in Whip.register too, so the prompt comes back after a whip_core restart, and it goes by itself when your resource stops. The same call puts an option on a car part or the F1 wheel: see Interactions.

7. Try it

  1. restart mycafe in the server console.
  2. Walk to the counter. The prompt appears; press E. $15 goes, a coffee arrives, and "Enjoy your coffee" pops up.
  3. Open /whip → System → Monitor. Its feed shows each mycafe:buy, accepted or refused, with the reason (a burst of identical refusals shows once every few seconds; the rest are counted).
  4. Drink the coffee: the bar runs with the cup in your hand, and the coffee leaves your pockets. With thirst switched on, the HUD's thirst ring goes up too.

If nothing happens, look at the server console and F8 for errors, and check each call's answer: a whip export that refuses answers false and a reason (see Return Patterns).

A picture for it. Until it has one, the inventory shows a placeholder. Put html/img/items/mycafe_coffee.webp in your resource and add files { 'html/img/items/*.webp' } to the manifest (see Item icons).

Your First Job

The coffee stand from Your First Resource, with staff: a job, a counter that offers different choices to customers and to staff on duty, coffee brewed under a bar the server times, and pay for each cup. About thirty minutes more, in the same four files.

8. The job

In server.lua, inside the same Whip.register function, declare the job. The first start makes it; every start after finds it again.

    -- The stand is a job: an owner and baristas
    local job, why = exports.whip_core:EnsureJob('mycafe', {
        name  = 'Bean Machine',
        roles = {
            { name = 'Owner',   level = 100 },
            { name = 'Barista', level = 1 },
        },
    })
    if not job then print('[mycafe] no job: ' .. tostring(why)) end

To hire yourself: /whip → Economy → Jobs, pick Bean Machine, Change, and hire yourself as a Barista. (A resource hires with HirePlayer.)

9. One counter, three choices

Customers buy; a barista clocks on, brews, clocks off. One prompt carries them all as options, each with its own require, so each player sees only theirs. In client.lua, the counter's AddAction becomes:

Whip.register(function()
    exports.whip_core:AddAction({
        id      = 'counter',
        at      = { coords = Config.Counter },
        options = {
            { id = 'buy', label = ('Buy coffee ($%d)'):format(Config.Price), icon = 'cash',
              onSelect = function() TriggerServerEvent('mycafe:buy') end },

            -- Staff only. whipJob is the job they are on duty at (false when off duty)
            { id = 'clockon', label = 'Clock on', require = { job = 'mycafe' },
              canInteract = function() return LocalPlayer.state.whipJob ~= 'mycafe' end,
              onSelect = function(ctx)
                  local ok, why = exports.whip_core:ClockOn('mycafe')
                  if not ok then ctx.refuse(why) end
              end },

            { id = 'brew', label = 'Brew a coffee', require = { job = 'mycafe', onDuty = true },
              onSelect = function() TriggerServerEvent('mycafe:brew') end },

            { id = 'clockoff', label = 'Clock off', require = { job = 'mycafe', onDuty = true },
              onSelect = function() exports.whip_core:ClockOff('mycafe') end },
        },
    })
end)

require only decides what each player is offered. Anything that matters is checked again on the server, as the brew below is.

10. Brewing, and pay

Add BrewPay = 5 to Config in shared.lua. Then, in server.lua's Whip.register:

    -- Brewing: staff on duty, at the counter, under a bar the server times; then a coffee, and their pay
    exports.whip_core:SecureEvent('mycafe:brew', {
        rateLimit = 2000,
        near = { at = Config.Counter, range = 3.0, message = 'Stand at the counter' },
    }, function(source, player)
        if not exports.whip_core:IsPlayerClockedOn(source, 'mycafe') then
            return false, 'Clock on first'
        end

        local done, reason = exports.whip_core:Progress(source, {
            label    = 'Brewing...',
            duration = 6000,
            near     = { coords = Config.Counter, range = 3.0 },   -- still at the counter when it ends
        })
        if not done then return false, reason end

        -- Six seconds went by: still the same character? (they may have logged out)
        if not exports.whip_core:IsSessionCurrent(source, player.session) then return end

        local given, gwhy = exports.whip_core:AddItem(source, 'mycafe_coffee', 1, nil, 'brewed')
        if not given then return false, gwhy end
        exports.whip_core:PayPlayer(source, Config.BrewPay, { reason = 'Brewed a coffee' })
    end)
  • The server checks the duty: require on the client only chose what was offered.
  • Progress on the server times the bar itself, so a modified game cannot skip it, and its own near means they must still be at the counter when it ends (the event's near is checked once, as it arrives).
  • IsSessionCurrent: a handler that waited checks the character it started with is still the one playing before it gives anything.
  • PayPlayer is the call for paying a player: what does not fit their pockets lands at their feet.

11. Try it

  1. restart mycafe, and hire yourself (step 8).
  2. At the counter: Buy coffee, and Clock on. Clock on, then Brew a coffee: a six-second bar, a coffee, $5.
  3. Walk away during the bar: it stops with "too far", and nothing is given.
  4. /whip → System → Monitor shows each mycafe:brew, and a refusal's reason.

The calls you'll use

whip has about 650 exports; a job, a shop or a mission uses about twenty of them. These are the ones whip's own resources call most, by task. The rest are there when you need them: the search box finds any.

ToCallSide

Make an item, and what using it doesRegisterItem, RegisterUseHandlerServer
Take a message from a player's game, checkedSecureEventServer
Answer a question from a player's game, checkedSecureCallback; ask it with CallbackServer; client
A prompt, a wheel option, a choice on a car partAddActionClient
A job, a stash, a shop that always existEnsureJob, EnsureContainer, EnsureShopServer
Players
Who is this (name, charId, job, session)GetPlayerServer
Tell them somethingNotifyPlayer; on their own game NotifyServer; client
Remember something about a characterSetPlayerFlag, GetPlayerFlagServer
Still the same character after a wait?IsSessionCurrentServer
Money
Charge for something, and undo it if what they paid for failsChargePlayer, RefundPlayerServer

Items

Do they have it, how manyHasItem, GetItemCountServer
Change one item (rounds, wear, a serial)SetItemMetadataServer
Move between any two places (pockets to a stash, to another player)StoreMoveServer

Hearing, being asked, saying no, declaring

whip talks to your resource in five ways. Which to use depends on what you want:

You wantUseExample
To hear that something happenedAn event: AddEventHandler('whip_core:…', fn). After the fact; you cannot stop it. On the server any resource can fire one, so check GetInvokingResource() where it matters (Server Events)whip_core:player:loaded
To hear a value change, from whip onlyA listener: OnStatChange, OnVehicleStatChange, WatchVehicleStat. Only whip calls it, and it goes when your resource stopsA HUD that follows hunger
A moment before whip does something on the player's gameA client hook: RegisterClientHook. whip waits for it (up to a second); it cannot say noPut your phone away before a gun is drawn
To say no to something of your ownA check you give with it: canUse, canInteract, a panel's onValidateNo drinking in a car
To add something to whipRegister…, Add…, Ensure…, inside Whip.registerRegisterItem, AddAction

Coming from QBCore, ESX or ox

whip is a whole framework of its own, and it currently has no bridge from QBCore, ESX or ox: there is no GetCoreObject, and a resource written for one of them does not run on whip unchanged. Porting a small job is a rewrite of its glue code (about a day), and most of what it wrote by hand is a single whip call. Start with How whip thinks; this page maps what you know.

Keep, replace, remove

ResourceWith whip
oxmysqlKeep: whip uses it. Ensure it above WHIP's resources
qb-core, es_extended, qbx_core, ox_coreRemove: one framework at a time. The setup report says when it finds one running
ox_inventory, qb-inventoryRemove: whip has its own (F2), and they need their framework to run
ox_target, qb-targetReplace with AddAction: prompts in the world, the F1 wheel, car parts
ox_libIts helpers (math, tables, lib.waitFor) are fine. For anything a player sees (notify, progress, input, menus), use whip's UI library: whip keeps one screen at a time, and ox_lib's do not know whip's are open
Garages, keys, fuel, banking, doorlock, housing, shops, multicharacter, spawn, HUDRemove: each is part of whip (below). Fuel is whip_fuel
A voice resource (pma-voice, mumble-voip)Remove if you use whip_voice; the setup report says when two run

Words and calls

QBCore / ESX / oxwhip
GetCoreObject(), ESX = exports.es_extended:getSharedObject()Nothing to fetch: dependency 'whip_core' and @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua in the manifest, then exports.whip_core:… (Your First Resource)
QBCore.Functions.GetPlayer(src), ESX.GetPlayerFromId(src)GetPlayer(source): a plain table (the player sheet), no methods: act through exports
PlayerData.citizenid, xPlayer.identifierplayer.charId (a number; save this one)
PlayerData.job, xPlayer.jobOn duty: GetPlayerJob(source) (nil while off duty). Has the job at all: GetPlayerRole(source, 'police')
PlayerData.gangNo gangs. A gang is a job made with EnsureJob: roles, a stash for its members, a bank account
PlayerData.metadataSetPlayerFlag, or SetPlayerMetadata (both while the character is on)
Player.Functions.AddMoney, xPlayer.addMoneyPayPlayer (cash, or method = 'bank')
Player.Functions.RemoveMoney, xPlayer.removeMoneyChargePlayer: answers a receipt for RefundPlayer
Cash as a number on the playerCash is an item, banknotes in the pockets: it can be dropped, stolen, put in a stash
shared/items.lua, ox_inventory/data/items.luaRegisterItem in your own resource, or /whip → Economy → Items
CreateUseableItem, ESX.RegisterUsableItemRegisterUseHandler; give it a table for a timed use (bar, animation, then onComplete)
Player.Functions.AddItem / RemoveItem, exports.ox_inventory:AddItemAddItem, RemoveItem; count with GetItemCount
A stash (ox_inventory:RegisterStash)EnsureContainer
RegisterNetEvent on the serverSecureEvent: rate limit, checked values, near (the event table)
CreateCallback / TriggerCallback, lib.callbackSecureCallback / Callback: return the answer, no cb
exports['qb-target']:AddBoxZone, ox_target:addSphereZone, addLocalEntityAddAction with at = { coords }, { entity }, { model }, { vehiclePart }; job = 'police' is require = { job = 'police' }, distance is reach
qb-menu, lib.registerContextNo list menu: options on a prompt (menus within a prompt), or a select field in Input
QBCore:Notify, lib.notify, showNotificationNotifyPlayer on the server, Notify on the client; or return false, 'why' from a SecureEvent
Progressbar, lib.progressBarProgress: on the server for anything handed out at the end (the server times it)
lib.skillCheck, lib.inputDialog, lib.alertDialogSkillCheck, Input, Alert / Confirm
lib.showTextUI, DrawText3DShowText on the client, ShowPlayerText from the server (an instruction band); usually a prompt (AddAction) says it already
PolyZone, lib.zonesZones (EnsureZone)
qb-vehiclekeys, SetFuel, qb-garagesGiveVehicleKey; the 'fuel' vehicle stat (whip_fuel); Garages. A car for a job: SpawnTempVehicle
QBCore.Functions.SetVehicleProperties(veh, props), lib.setVehicleProperties(veh, props)SetVehicleProperties({ entity = veh }, props) on the client. In whip a bare number is a vehicleId, so the entity goes in a table; a bare entity is refused with that hint. To keep the look, SetVehicleAppearance on the server
AddBlipForCoord + SetBlipRouteShowBlip from the server, with route = true
qb-doorlock, ox_doorlockEnsureDoors (Doors)
Lang:t(), localesNo locale system: your resource's text is your own

What will surprise you

  • Everything you declare goes in Whip.register, not at the top of a file (the one rule).
  • "Their job" means on duty. GetPlayerJob is nil while a player is off duty; ask GetPlayerRole for "works there at all". Players clock themselves on and off in the phone's Business app, and your resource can put them on duty with ClockOn, on the server or from a prompt at the station. A job with selfClockOn = false is on duty only when your code says so.
  • Pay with PayPlayer. Cash is banknotes; AddPlayerCash, the low-level call, refuses when the pockets are full.
  • A receipt lasts 30 minutes. Refund a van deposit within the job; at the end of a long shift, give it back with PayPlayer.
  • A bar on the player's game is their word. Anything handed out at the end runs the server's Progress, or a declared timed use.
  • Exports answer false, 'why' instead of throwing, and a SecureEvent handler that answers false, 'why' shows the player why (Return Patterns).
  • No gangs, no list menu, no locales (above).

A qb delivery job, call by call

The qb job doesThe whip version does
A job in shared/jobs.luaEnsureJob('delivery', { … }) in Whip.register
qb-target box at the depot, job = 'delivery'AddAction({ at = { coords = DEPOT }, require = { job = 'delivery', onDuty = true }, … })
Deposit for the van: RemoveMoney('bank', 500)ChargePlayer(source, 500, { method = 'bank' }), keep the receipt
CreateVehicle + vehiclekeys + SetFuelSpawnTempVehicle: a key for the driver, and the van goes when you despawn it, after despawnAfter, or when your resource stops
Packages: AddItem + ItemBoxStoreGive into the van's boot, or AddItem
Blip and route to the drop-offShowBlip({ people = { source } }, 'drop', { coords = DROP, route = true })
Progressbar at the door, then TriggerServerEvent('delivery:pay')A prompt at the door; a SecureEvent with near on the drop-off runs the server Progress, takes the package, pays
Pay: AddMoney('cash', 120)PayPlayer(source, 120, { reason = 'Delivery' })
Van back: refund the depositRefundPlayer(receipt) within 30 minutes; after that PayPlayer

The near check closes the classic delivery-job exploit: firing the pay event from anywhere on the map.

The whole job, written out, is whip_core/docs/examples/whip_delivery_example: sign on, clock on, the van and its deposit, packages in the boot, a route to each door, pay at the door, the deposit back, and what happens when the driver logs out or the van is taken back. Copy the folder into your resources folder and ensure it to run it.

Return Patterns

One rule: the first answer is the result, or false; the second is why. Never nil, 'reason': an export's answers are cut off at the first nil, so the reason would never arrive. By kind of call:

CategorySuccessFailure
Mutatingtrue, or the useful thing: where it went, the slot, what was takenfalse, 'reason'
Read (player)valueA list, a count or a yes/no answers its empty form and why: {}, 'Player not loaded' · 0, 'Player not loaded' · false, 'Player not loaded'. A single value (a stat, a metadata key, coordinates, the sheet) answers nil: an export cannot carry a reason after a nil
Check (may they?)truefalse, 'reason': CanUseBankAccount, CanUseGarage, HasPropertyAccess, HasJobPermission, IsAuthorizedForDoor
Createtable (the new thing), except a vehicle, which answers its vehicleId (CreateOwnedVehicle, SpawnTempVehicle, AdoptVehicle): every vehicle export and event names a car by its id, and you will key your own tables by it. GetVehicle(vehicleId) is the tablefalse, 'reason'
Deletetruefalse, 'reason'
Lookuptablenil when there is nothing, and false, 'reason' when the question itself is wrong (a bad address)
Error checking: always capture both return values: local ok, err = exports.whip_core:RemoveItem(...). A few calls answer something more useful than true when they work: AddItem says where the item went ('inventory' or 'ground'), and StoreGive says the slot it landed in. That value is still truthy, so if not ok then reads the same.

Is the reason a code or a sentence?

Two kinds of why, and each call's card says which it gives:

KindLooks likeCallsUse it to
A codeshort, lower case: 'busy', 'cancelled', 'too far', 'failed'Progress, SkillCheck (both sides)Branch on it: if why == 'cancelled' then. Write your own words for the player.
A sentencewritten for a person: 'Not enough cash', 'They are not online: …'Everything else: money, items, keys, jobs, vehicles, doors, propertiesShow it: Notify(source, why, 'error'), or answer it from a SecureEvent handler. Don't compare it, as the words may change.

A call that hands back an id answers the id, or false and why: AddAction, AddPoint, HoldMoney, WatchVehicleStat. Where there is a third answer (the warnings of AddAction, UpdateAction and AddPoint), the second is false rather than nothing on success, so the third gets through the export.

Naming a person: a server id, or { charId = n }

Wherever an export takes a person (whose bank account, who gets the key, who is hiring, whose pockets), it takes the same two things: a bare number is a server id (the source your handler already holds), and a character, online or not, is { charId = n }. A bare number is never a charId. The one exception is an export whose own name says what it takes: GetCharacterProperties(charId), GetPlayerFromCharId(charId).

exports.whip_core:GivePropertyKey(propertyId, source)              -- the player in front of you
exports.whip_core:GivePropertyKey(propertyId, { charId = 42 })  -- a character, online or not
A server id must be online. One that is not is refused with a reason that says so. To reach a character who may be offline, pass { charId = n }. A few calls need the person online whichever way you name them, because what they hand over goes into their pockets or onto a live record (a car key, TransferVehicle); those say so on their cards, and refuse an offline character with a reason. A parameter named source (not who) is always a server id.

Two things the export boundary does to your values

Both come from FiveM, not whip, and neither gives an error where the mistake is, so they are worth knowing before you meet them.

1. A function that crosses an export is callable, but its type() is not "function".

It arrives as a reference. Calling it works normally, so passing a callback to any whip export is fine. What breaks is testing one: 
-- WRONG — false for every callback that came through an export
if type(fn) == 'function' then ...

-- RIGHT — check what you can identify, and let pcall settle the rest
if fn ~= nil then pcall(fn, ...) end
This matters when you write an export that accepts a function. Type-check it and you will reject every caller, return false to all of them, and see nothing in the console.
2. A nil returned through an export arrives as no values at all.

The trailing nil is dropped from the return list, so nesting the call inside anything that requires an argument calls it with none: 
-- WRONG — errors with "bad argument #1 to 'type' (value expected)"
if type(exports.whip_core:GetVehicleData(id, 'key')) == 'table' then ...

-- RIGHT — a local absorbs the empty return as nil
local data = exports.whip_core:GetVehicleData(id, 'key')
if type(data) == 'table' then ...
It only fails on the path where the value is absent, so it survives every test that happens to find something. Assign export results to a local before using them.

Registering things with whip: one rule for all of them

Items, stats, secure events, callbacks, panel items, store kinds, context actions, item flags, theme overrides, zones: everything a resource registers with whip follows the same rule:

You register…What happens
something newIt is yours. Answers true.
the same thing againNothing happens: no re-broadcast, no reset. So running your registration twice is always safe.
a changed version of your ownIt replaces yours.
something another resource registeredRefused: false, 'item "x" belongs to other_resource'. Nothing is taken over quietly, and every refusal is said once in the console (F8 for a game's), naming your resource, so one you did not check is still seen. The setup report lists them.
a name starting whip_core:Refused: those are whip's own, even ones it has not used yet.

When your resource stops, what it registered is removed (items are the exception, since players are still carrying them, but they stop being yours, so another resource may take the name). Removing something only ever removes your own. exports.whip_core:GetRegistrations(resource?) lists who holds what, on the side you call it from. Handy when a registration is refused and you want to see who has the name.

Names: start them with your resource's name

Some lists are one for the whole server: item keys, right-click action names, stats, vehicle stats, server zone ids and permissions. The first resource to register a name owns it, so two sellers who both call their item nitro clash, and which one starts first wins. Start every name with your resource's name and an underscore: mycafe_coffee, mycafe_stress, mycafe_manage. (Events and callbacks take a colon, mycafe:buy, as FiveM's own do.) A name that does not start that way still works; the server console says so once, in one line listing them:

[whip_core] mycafe registers 3 items whose names do not start with "mycafe" (coffee, bagel, tea). Every resource shares one list of them, ...
Names whip's own resources already hold, without a prefix: items phone, sim_card (whip_phone), rope (whip_rope), radio, megaphone (whip_voice), nitro (whip_autos), and whip_gunny's guns, magazines and ammo (its Config.Weapons, named after GTA's: weapon_pistol); the vehicle stats nitro, boost, fuel; and every item in whip_core's config.lua. Pick other names for yours; /whip → Economy → Items shows each key's owner.

What you have registered, and run tags

Two tools for what a resource holds: a list of every registration (for finding out who holds a name that was refused), and run tags, which let a mission or a heist clean up everything it made in one call.

GetRegistrations(resource)CLIENTSERVER

Everything registered with whip on this side (events, callbacks, items, stats, actions …, and the stat listeners, client hooks, settings and /w pages, debug tools and held props), or only one resource's share. Handy when a registration is refused and you want to see who holds the name.

ParamTypeDescription
resourcestring|nilOnly this resource's registrations; everything when left out
for _, r in ipairs(exports.whip_core:GetRegistrations(GetCurrentResourceName())) do
    print(r.registry, r.key)
end
Returns: table[]: { { registry, key, owner }, … }
ReleaseTag(tag)CLIENTSERVER

Removes everything your resource registered under one run tag, in every whip module, and closes the tag: anything registered under it afterwards is refused with "… has ended". A registration takes a tag in its options table, { tag = 'run:42' }, on the modules that support it. Use a new tag for each run (a mission, a heist): releasing one run never touches another, and never touches another resource's things, even under the same tag. When your resource stops, its closed tags are forgotten.

ParamTypeDescription
tagstringYour run's label, e.g. 'run:42' (up to 100 characters)
local tag = 'heist:' .. jobId
exports.whip_core:SpawnNpc({ model = 's_m_m_security_01', coords = guardPos, behaviour = 'guard' }, { tag = tag })
exports.whip_core:SpawnTempVehicle('stockade', vanPos, { tag = tag })

-- The job is over: the guard and the van go, and nothing more can be made under the tag
local ok, count = exports.whip_core:ReleaseTag(tag)
Returns: true, count: how many things went; or false, reason for an empty or over-long tag
ListTagged(tag)CLIENTSERVER

What your resource holds under one run tag, across whip's modules.

ParamTypeDescription
tagstringYour run's label
Returns: table[]: { { registry, key }, … }; empty for an unknown or bad tag

The satellite helper: @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua

A file your resource includes. It runs in your resource rather than being an export, because it has to remember your registrations across a whip_core restart.

-- fxmanifest.lua
dependency 'whip_core'
shared_script '@whip_core/lib/satellite.lua'

A whip_core restart, with and without the dependency. With dependency 'whip_core' (every whip resource, and the normal case), FiveM stops your resource first when whip_core stops, and whip_core starts it again once it is back (Your First Resource, step 1). Your resource starts fresh: Whip.register runs on that start, and there is nothing to clean up. Without the dependency (a resource that also runs with no whip at all), your resource keeps running: Whip.onCoreLost runs when whip_core stops, Whip.register runs again when it is back, and Whip.call answers false, 'whip_core stopped' to a call that was waiting. Whip.call matters either way: early in a start, and on a player's game while whip_core is still loading, it answers false, why where a straight call would throw.

What else it does in your resource. So whip's tools can show your errors (GetErrorLog, the Monitor), it wraps CreateThread, Citizen.CreateThreadNow, SetTimeout, RegisterCommand, AddStateBagChangeHandler, RegisterNUICallback and print in your resource. They work exactly as before, and any error (or red ^1 print) is also handed to whip_core. The cost is about half a microsecond per event handler. To turn it off, add whip_error_tap 'no' to your fxmanifest; the rest of the helper works the same.

Autocomplete for every whip export. Copy whip_core/types/luarc.template.json into your resource's folder as .luarc.json, open the folder in VS Code with the Lua extension (sumneko), and every exports.whip_core:... call, and Whip.*, shows its parameters and what it returns. It looks for whip's types next to your resource (../whip_core/types) and next to a [whip] folder (../[whip]/whip_core/types); for any other layout, change that path. It also knows the fxmanifest's words, so your manifest is not underlined.
CallWhat it does
Whip.register(fn)Runs fn when whip_core is ready (whichever of you started first) and again every time whip_core restarts. Put everything you register with whip in it. Works on server and client.
Whip.onCoreLost(fn)Only for a resource without dependency 'whip_core' (with it, your resource stops first and this never runs). Runs fn when whip_core stops: to let go of something that only made sense while it ran (a UI you opened through it). Registrations need no cleanup. Every player has been logged out by then, and no whip_core:player:logout fires for them, so drop per-player state here too; whip_core:player:loaded fires for each again when whip_core is back.
Whip.registry(name, opts) · Whip.caller()A registry of your own with whip's registration rule, for a resource others extend (phone apps, MDT plugins, tuning parts): an entry is its first registrant's, the same again changes nothing, another resource's is refused and said once in your console, and a resource's entries go when it stops. local Apps = Whip.registry('app', { label = 'app' }), then in your export return Apps:add(Whip.caller(), id, def); read Apps.entries, Apps:get(id), Apps:keysOf(owner).
Whip.requires('1.0') · Whip.has(name)Which whip your resource needs. Put whip_requires '1.0' in your fxmanifest.lua and the setup report prints a FIX line when the server's whip_core is older; Whip.requires says the same from your code (once, and answers false). Whip.has('GetBalance') asks whether this whip_core has one call, for a feature newer than the oldest whip you support.
Whip.command(name, opts, fn) (server)A command a player types, behind the same gate as a SecureEvent: refused while they are down (whileDead = true allows it), rate limited (three at once, then one a second; rateLimit = false for none), ace = 'my.perm' for an ACE, and dev = true for the server console and whip.devtools with developer mode on. A refusal is said to the player; fn(source, args, raw) runs in its own thread. Whip.command('ropes', { dev = true }, function(source) … end). Use it instead of a bare RegisterCommand with your own checks.
Whip.registerWith(resource, fn)The other side: runs fn now if resource is running and again each time it starts, so registering with another resource's registry survives its restart (Whip.registerWith('whip_phone', function() exports.whip_phone:RegisterModule(…) end)).
Whip.call(name, …)Calls a whip export safely: Whip.call('AddItem', source, 'cookie', 1). Answers what the export answers, or false, reason when whip_core is down or the call errored, never an error in your code. Use it around an export that waits, on the player (Progress, SkillCheck) or on the database (ChargePlayer, the Ensure* calls, on the client Callback and ResolveVehicle), while you hold a flag, a lock or a half-done step: if whip_core stops mid-wait it answers false, 'whip_core stopped', where a direct call never returns. That means "no answer", not "did not happen". A charge already sent may still land, so check before you repeat it. Not for per-frame code: there, call a quick export straight, behind Whip.isReady().
Whip.core:Name(…)Whip.call with the export's own types: Whip.core:AddItem(source, 'cookie', 1) is Whip.call('AddItem', source, 'cookie', 1), and your editor shows its params and answers (with the .luarc.json above), where Whip.call('Name') shows none and a misspelt name only answers false.
Whip.ready(timeoutMs?)Waits (inside a thread) until whip_core is ready. false if it timed out.
Whip.voice(name, …) · Whip.voiceSystem()Calls whichever voice system runs (whip_voice, or a voice resource of your own) and says which it is. See Voice for other resources.
Whip.isReady()Is whip_core running and ready right now?

Calling whip_core: one rule

Where the call isCallWhy
Inside a handler whip_core runs: SecureEvent, SecureCallback, a use handler, a right-click action, a hook, Whip.register itselfexports.whip_core:Name(…)whip_core is up while it runs. Inside a SecureEvent, a payment and what it pays for are written together
Code of your own: a thread, a command, a timer, an NUI callback, a net event of your own, client code at a key pressWhip.core:Name(…)whip_core may not be up yet (early in a start; on a player's game still loading). It answers false, why where a straight call would throw
Code that runs every frameexports.whip_core:Name(…) behind Whip.isReady(), a quick export onlyWhip.core starts a thread per call: too much 60 times a second

Both answer the same things: Whip.core only adds false, why for "whip_core is not there". An export whose card says WAITS can wait (on the database, or on the player): call it from a thread or a handler, never at file scope, and after it returns, read again anything that may have changed meanwhile (an item may have moved). Your editor shows the same exports as async.

The whip way

The rules whip's own resources keep, and why. A resource that keeps them works on every server whip runs on, survives a whip_core restart, and does not fight other resources.

RuleWhy
Declare inside Whip.register. Items, events, actions, jobswhip_core keeps them in memory and forgets them when it restarts. The one rule
The server decides; the game only asks. Every message from a game is a SecureEvent or SecureCallback that names its values, and near where it mattersA modified game can send anything, from anywhere, as often as it likes. Secure Events
Answer false, 'why'. Never throw, never a bare nilThe caller can tell a refusal from a bug, and the player can read why. Return Patterns
Save a charId, never a server idA server id changes every time someone joins and is handed to the next player. How whip thinks
Ask whip for what players share: the screen (SetUIOpen), the controls (BlockControls), the hands (FreeHands), the pedOne owner each, so two resources never fight over the same thing, and each lets go when its resource stops. Screens, input and controls
React to events, do not poll. No while true do Wait(0) to watch for a change: listen for the event, or wait on the call that answersA loop every frame costs every player all the time; an event costs nothing until it happens. Timing your loops
One call per action. StoreMove, not RemoveItem then AddItem; your own table written after SavePlayerWhat one action changes is written in one transaction, so a crash never leaves it half done. Save System
Name things after your resource: mycafe_coffee, mycafe:buyNames are server-wide and first come, first served; another resource's name is refused. The registration rule
Put a rule where every path passes. A check in your export, not in each callerThe next caller cannot forget it, and an exception is something a caller asks for, not a hole it finds.
Settings on a page, not in code. Whip.configPage for anything a server owner might changeOwners are often not coders: they change it in /whip, and it survives your updates. Settings pages

What a resource can change

Almost everything is done from your own resource, without editing whip_core, so whip's updates never undo your work. Here is where the line is.

Without touching whip_core

You canWith
Add things: items, stats, prompts, jobs, shops, stashes, kinds of storage, item windows, settings pages, Director cards, /w pages, skill check games, a voice systemRegister…, Add…, Ensure… in Whip.register (The calls you'll use)
Change whip's own rules a server owner might want different/whip → Settings → Config, or config.lua: the respawn wait and hospitals, what empty hunger costs, the lockpick game, whether getting out unlocks a car, the character screen's fades, and some 200 more (Configuration)
Hold one of whip's things for a whileHoldRespawn (a dead player waits for a medic), HoldVehicleEngine, BlockControls, BlockHands, HoldPlayerPed
Say no to something of yourscanUse, canInteract, a panel's onValidate (Hearing, being asked, saying no)
Hear what happenedServer Events, Client Events

What a resource cannot change

  • whip's own items' uses (the lockpick, the bandage, food and drink): they are whip_core's, and a resource cannot take one over. Register an item of your own instead, or change the item in /whip → Economy → Items.
  • The status HUD (the gauges bottom left): your stats add gauges (RegisterStat with hud), and Config.HudSkin picks one of two looks, but it cannot be turned off or drawn by your resource. It also carries notifications and the chat line.
  • The spawn picker's choices: where they last were, the presets in config.lua, and their homes.

Replacing a screen

ScreenHow
The look of every screenA theme: a resource with a theme.css, chosen by Config.Theme or live with SetActiveTheme (Theming & Skins)
InventoryThe renderer seat: Config.InventoryRenderer names your resource, which draws it while whip runs it (the seat)
Death screenConfig.DeathScreen = false, and draw your own from whip_core:death:screenChanged (Death & Revive)
Phonewhip_phone is a resource like yours: stop it and run your own, which takes the screen with SetUIOpen, its corner with SetUIArea, and the hands with FreeHands
Chatwhip_chat answers the stock chat's events; any chat resource that does works instead
Loading screenAny FiveM loading screen resource; whip_core closes it when the player arrives (the setup report says when two run)
Status HUD, character select, character creator, spawn picker, notifications, progress barA theme only (above)

Testing your resource

What whip gives you to try your resource before a player does, alone and with one game.

To test…Use
Your inventory screen, with no gameThe preview: node whip_core/dev/inventory-preview/preview.js my_inventory_ui runs your screen in Chrome with sample scenes, a "Refuse next move" button and a log of what your screen sent (the renderer seat)
A Director cardTestDirectorCard(type, props, { player = source }) runs its real code once as a Test, and TestDirectorScenario a whole scenario (Director cards)
Something done to another player, aloneName a character who is not online: every export that takes a person takes { charId = n } (Naming a person). A key, a payment or a permission given to a second character of your own shows up when you log in as them
Two players at onceRun two FiveM clients on one PC. Both log in as the same account, each with its own character. Money between two characters of one account is refused while Config.BlockOwnCharacterTransfers is on (the default): turn it off on a test server
Dying, healing, a broken car/w → Kill Me, Restore Health & Armour, Repair Vehicle (Dev Tools)
What your events did/whip → System → Monitor: each SecureEvent call, accepted or refused, with the reason and how long your handler took
Errors you didn't see/w → Resources, or whiperrors in the server console: your resource's latest errors and refusals on each side. In code, GetErrorLog before and after a test

Measuring your resource

How much your resource costs, on the player's game and on the server, before a busy server finds out for you.

WhereToolWhat it tells you
The player's game/whipcost (developer mode)Each timed section's microseconds per frame and each resource's memory, for 5 to 120 seconds, the dearest first. Time your own loops with local t = WhipCost.start() … WhipCost.stop('my loop', t) (client_script '@whip_core/lib/cost.lua'; never a Wait between the two) and they show up there by name
The player's gameMeasureFrames({ seconds })Frames per second, the worst 1 %, and how many frames took over 33 and 50 ms, to compare with your resource started and stopped
The serverwhipcost [seconds] in the server consoleThe same table for the server: each section you mark with WhipCost.start / WhipCost.stop (server_script '@whip_core/lib/cost.lua'), its runs a second, microseconds a run and milliseconds of the server's CPU a second. Time only, by the server's CPU clock; never a Wait between the two
The server/whip → System → MonitorHow long each of your SecureEvent and SecureCallback handlers took. It is time on the clock, so a database wait counts in it
Either sideFiveM's profiler: profiler record 500 in F8 (the game) or the server console, then profiler viewEvery resource's time, frame by frame, in Chrome's performance view. Look for your resource's name under each frame; a tall block is a slow tick. With setr whip_profiling 1 whip_core's own handlers are named after their events. A profiler capture makes everything look about five times dearer than it is: compare captures with each other, not with a budget

A loop that runs every frame (Wait(0)) is the usual cost. Wait on an event or a promise instead (the whip way), and use /whipcost to check the loops you must keep.

What an export costs

Every export is one of these, cheapest first. Call the first two as often as you need; the last three when something happens, never every frame.

CostFor exampleWhat it means
MemoryHasItem, GetItemCount, IsPlayerClockedOn, GetPlayerJob, GetBalance after its first readAnswered from what whip already holds: microseconds
A copyGetPlayer, GetVehicle, StoreReadFrom memory too, but every table an export answers is packed and unpacked on its way to you, so a big table costs more than a number. Keep the part you need rather than asking for the whole table every frame. GetVehicle with { occupants = true } also walks every player
Sends to a gameNotifyPlayer, ShowBlip, ShowPlayerText, SetPlayerMetadataA message to that player's game, or to every game: bytes on their connection. Right for an action; wrong in a loop over every player every second
Waits on the databaseThe Ensure* calls, bank reads, ChargePlayer, PayPlayer, AddItem, SetVehicleDataThe card says WAITS. Milliseconds, more on a busy database: call it from a thread or a handler, and afterwards read again anything that may have changed meanwhile
Waits on the other side, or on the playerProgress and SkillCheck on the server; Callback, ResolveVehicle and Input on the clientWAITS too: a round trip between the game and the server (200 ms at 200 ms ping), or as long as the player takes

Writing for both platforms

One whip runs on GTA V Legacy and on GTA V Enhanced, and so can your resource. Almost everything is the same. These are the places it is not:

WhatOn EnhancedDo this
Another player in this gameGetPlayerFromServerId answers 0, not -1, for a player this game does not have, and 0 can be a real player, often youlocal idx = Whip.playerIndex(serverId): nil when they are not in this game (lib/satellite.lua)
Models, maps, streamed propsA model built for Legacy must be convertedOne resource with both: stream/ for Legacy and stream_enhanced/ for Enhanced, which streams it instead of stream/ when it is there. whip's own resources are packed this way
NPCs made at startOne made before any character has loaded can lose its network id to a player or a car (the console says so)Make NPCs after whip_core:player:loaded, or in Whip.register once a player is on
A wide DUI pageCreateDui refuses a page wider than 8192 pixelsPack an atlas into rows, not one long strip
Anything elseexports.whip_core:GetPlatform() answers 'legacy' or 'enhanced' on either side

Selling on whip

Your resource is yours

whip_core and whip's own resources are licensed under the GNU LGPL 3.0 (each resource's COPYING.LESSER, with the GPL 3.0 it builds on in COPYING; whip_core's emote list, shared/emote_list.lua, is GPL 3.0). A resource that uses whip through its exports, and loads @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua from whip_core's own folder, is your own work: open or closed, free or sold, under any licence you choose. That is whip's reading of its licence, not legal advice.

Do not copy whip's files into your resource. A file copied out of whip stays LGPL, and whoever has your resource must be able to change it, which an encrypted copy does not allow. Load the helper with shared_script '@whip_core/lib/satellite.lua'; never paste it in. The example resources (names ending in _example or _examples) are the exception: they are under the MIT licence, so copy from them freely.

Don't call your resource whip. The licence covers whip's code, not its name or logo: a fork or a modified copy must not use them in a way that suggests it is whip. Saying your resource works with whip is fine. whip_core/NOTICE.md lists the parts whip's licence does not cover: the Rockstar Games material and the third-party code, fonts and data, each with its own terms.

Escrow

FiveM's asset escrow encrypts your Lua. whip never reads or runs your Lua files: it knows your resource by its name as you call it (GetInvokingResource), and your settings live in whip's database. A few files must stay readable:

FileWith escrow
Your config.luaIn escrow_ignore, so the owner can edit it. A Whip.configPage lets them change it in /whip instead
A property pack as .luaIn escrow_ignore, or ship it as .json. An encrypted one is refused with that advice
Director scenario packs.json already: nothing to do
Your page (ui_page), images, soundsEscrow leaves them as they are

whip is untested with escrowed resources. If something of yours stops working once encrypted, send the console's lines.

What a buyer can copy

Escrow protects Lua and streamed models. Everything that is data stays readable on the buyer's server: your page's HTML, JavaScript and CSS, images, sounds, property packs, and Director scenarios. A scenario you ship can be duplicated in the buyer's Director and exported as a pack. Price a scenario pack knowing that.

Glossary

The words these docs use in a sense of their own, one line each. The link goes to where each is explained. Where QBCore, ESX or ox has its own word for the same thing, it is given as Elsewhere.

WordMeans
ACEFiveM's own permission system, set in server.cfg with add_ace. whip.devtools is the ACE for whip's admin tools. Dev Tools
ActionSomething a player can do: a prompt they walk up to, an option on the F1 wheel, or a choice on a car part. Made with AddAction. Elsewhere: a target option (qb-target, ox_target). Interactions
AddressHow a store, and a slot in it, is named: { kind, id, sub, slot }. Addresses
AudienceWho something the server shows is for (a blip, a prop set, a point), or whom an NPC fights: 'everyone' (not for an NPC), or { people = { serverId | { charId = n } } }. Player
charIdOne character's id. It is saved, so it stays the same across restarts, and an account can have several characters. Naming a person
Consume, liveThe two ways a client reports a vehicle stat only it can know: how much was used (fuel, nitrous), or what it is worth now (boost, heat). The server caps both. consume and live
CardOne step of a Director scenario: an NPC, a car, a goal, a line of talk. A resource can add its own with RegisterDirectorCard. Director cards
ContainerA storage box placed in the world, often called a stash. One kind of store. Elsewhere: a stash. Containers
Developer modeA switch in /w for admins. With it off an admin plays as a player: whip's admin tools and whip.devtools checks treat them as one, so nothing is done by accident. Dev Tools
Directorwhip's scenario maker in /whip: missions, heists and stories built from cards on a canvas, run for players, no code needed. The Director
DUIA web page drawn onto something in the world (a screen, a sign, a stat card above a car) instead of over the game. DUI
Ensure…EnsureJob, EnsureShop, EnsureDoors, EnsureZone and the rest: declare that something exists. The first call makes it; later calls find it and bring it in line with what you declare now (EnsureDoors also releases a door whose key you took off the list). Safe in Whip.register on every start. Jobs
F1 wheelThe radial menu a player opens with F1 (or holding D-pad down). Options on it are actions with at = { radial = true }. Elsewhere: a radial menu (qb-radialmenu, ox_lib's radial). at: where it lives
Ground itemAn item lying in the world, dropped or thrown. Not a store: it has its own exports. Elsewhere: a drop. Ground Items
HookA function of yours whip asks at a set moment and waits for: a panel's onValidate and onChange around a move (panel hooks), or a client moment such as 'freeHands' (RegisterClientHook). Unlike an event, a hook can answer, and some can say no.
Item keyThe name an item is registered under, such as 'mycafe_coffee'. Item Definition
LayerA named change stacked on top of something, so that taking it off restores what was under it. A weather layer changes the time or weather one player sees (Layers); a handling layer changes how a car drives (SetVehicleHandlingLayer).
Lore characterA story person the Director keeps: a name, a face, a phone, a bank name, voice lines. Scenarios use them again and again, and they can text, call and pay players. The Director
Managed doorA saved door that a resource or a system owns: one declared with EnsureDoors, or a home's door. Admins can rename it but not change who opens it, and a declared door's rename is put back when its resource next starts. Doors
MonitorThe /whip section that lists every SecureEvent and SecureCallback call, accepted or refused, with Sentinel's detections. Dev Tools
nearA SecureEvent and SecureCallback rule: the call is refused unless the player is within range of a fixed spot, a position worked out from the call, or the car it names. Checking where they are
Owned and session vehiclesOwned: someone's car, saved in the database. Session: any other car whip knows, kept in memory only: a street or NPC car, or a temporary car your resource made with SpawnTempVehicle (a rental, a job van), which goes when your resource stops. Vehicles & Keys
PanelAn inventory-like window your resource opens beside the player's inventory, with OpenPanel: a crafting bench, an evidence locker. Elsewhere: a secondary inventory. Panels
Panel itemAn item that holds other items, such as a wallet or a toolbox. Made with RegisterPanelItem. Panels
PermissionA whip staff role given to a player's account while the server runs, for things between everyone and full admins. Declared with RegisterPermission, given with GrantPermission. Not the same as an ACE. Permissions
PersonWherever an export takes a person: the player's server id for someone online, or { charId = n } for a character online or not. Naming a person
Player sheetThe plain table GetPlayer answers, and the player a SecureEvent handler receives: fields such as charId and fullName, no methods. Elsewhere: PlayerData (QBCore), xPlayer (ESX), but with no methods. Player
PocketsA player's own stores: the main inventory (sub = 'player') and the accessory strip ('accessory'). Elsewhere: the player's inventory. Addresses
PointAn interaction point added by server code while it runs (AddPoint).
Presencepersist = 'presence' on a vehicle stat: the database remembers that the car has it, at the value it was fitted with, and not each change after. RegisterVehicleStat
ReceiptWhat ChargePlayer answers when the player paid. Hand it to RefundPlayer to give the money back. Charging a Player
RegistryWhat whip_core keeps in memory of everything resources have declared: items, use handlers, actions, events. Forgotten when whip_core restarts, which is why declarations go in Whip.register. What you have registered
Registration ruleRegistering the same thing again changes nothing, a changed version of your own replaces it, and another resource's name is refused. The rule
Run tagA label such as 'run:42' given to what one mission makes, so ReleaseTag removes all of it in one call. Run tags
SatelliteAny resource built on whip_core, yours included. It loads @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua for Whip.register. Elsewhere: a script, a resource. The satellite helper
SecureEvent, SecureCallbackRegisterNetEvent, and a server answer to a client's question, with the checks built in: rate limit, checked values, near, ownership, ACE and permissions. Secure Events
Sentinelwhip's guard against a player's game changing the statebags whip writes about them or their car: it puts the value back and strikes the player. Sentinel
Session (a character's)A number on the player sheet, new each time a character loads. A handler that waited checks it with IsSessionCurrent before it gives or takes anything. Not the same as a session vehicle. IsSessionCurrent
Setup reportWhat whip_core prints in the server console as it starts: what it found wrong with this server's setup (the database version, a missing resource, a stock resource that clashes) and the line that fixes each. Quick Start
Server id, sourceThe number FiveM gives a connected player. It changes every time they join, so save a charId, never a source. Naming a person
Stat, effectA character's numbers that whip keeps on the server (health, armour, hunger, thirst and any a resource registers) and timed changes to them (ApplyEffect). Not the same as a vehicle stat. Stats & Effects
SnapshotThe table GetVehicle answers: a copy of what whip knows about a car at that moment. It names the car too, so it can be handed back to any vehicle export. Vehicle references
StatebagFiveM's way of sharing facts about a player or an entity with every player's game. whip puts a few there (whipDead, a car's stats) for games to draw from, and keeps its own record on the server. Sentinel
StoreAnywhere items sit: pockets, a container, a car's boot, glovebox or ignition, a shop, a panel item. Every store moves items the same way. Elsewhere: an inventory (ox_inventory's word for all of these). Not the same as a shop. Stores
Store kindWhich sort of store an address names: 'player', 'container', 'vehicle' and others. A resource can declare its own. Store Kinds
Use handlerWhat happens when a player uses an item: a function, or a table that runs a timed use (a bar, an animation, then onComplete). Given with RegisterUseHandler. Elsewhere: a usable item (QBCore's CreateUseableItem, ESX's RegisterUsableItem). RegisterUseHandler
userIdA player's account, made the first time they connect. It can hold up to Config.MaxCharacters characters; permissions are given to the account. Character Lifecycle
Vehicle dataAnything stuck to a car that is not a gauge: a fitted part's grade, a finance flag. SetVehicleData. Vehicle Data
Vehicle referenceHow a car is named to an export: { id = vehicleId }, { entity = veh }, { plate = … } or { netId = … }. A bare number is a vehicleId. Vehicle references
Vehicle statA gauge on a car that whip keeps, syncs and saves: fuel, nitrous, a turbo's boost. Declared with RegisterVehicleStat. RegisterVehicleStat
vehicleIdwhip's own id for a car: the database's number for an owned car, 1,000,000,000 and up for the rest. Not the entity handle, not the netId. Vehicles & Keys
WatcherWatchVehicleStat (or WatchVehicleData): your code runs when a car in range gains or loses a stat, and while one carries it, or only while you drive it, with driverOnly. Watching Vehicle Stats
Whip.registerThe function your resource hands everything it declares to whip, so whip can run it again after a whip_core restart. Your First Resource, step 3

Secure Events

whip guards three doors. What a player's game sends your server: Secure Events, here. What it writes to the facts every game shares: the Sentinel. And who may do what: Permissions.

Any player can send your server any event, with any values, as often as they like. That is all a cheat menu needs: TriggerServerEvent('myshop:buy', 'gold_bar', -50). Most FiveM exploits are a server event that believed what it was sent. The callbacks in ESX, QBCore and ox_lib deliver the call; checking what is in it is left to every resource, every time.

SecureEvent is how whip stops that. Beside your handler, you write down what a call must look like: how often a player may send it, what each value must be, where they must be standing, what they must own. whip checks all of it before your code runs. A call that fails never reaches you: it is refused, and the Monitor shows who sent it and why. SecureCallback does the same for a question the client asks and waits on.

Before and after

A purchase with RegisterNetEvent, checked by hand:

local lastBuy = {}

RegisterNetEvent('myshop:buy', function(itemKey, amount)
    local source = source
    local player = exports.whip_core:GetPlayer(source)
    if not player or player.isDead then return end                -- loaded, and alive
