NPC Runs Away · NPC Plays Emote · NPC Walks To · NPC Follows PlayerWhat an NPC the run made (or its whole group) does: runs from this player or the nearest of them and stops fighting; plays an emote (/e names) over and over, empty to stop; walks or runs to a placed thing and stays there (Arrived, Did not get there when it dies or goes); walks after the player, an escort ("stop following" leaves it where it is)

A card that waits on the server gives up out of Took too long.

Placing things in the world

Each placed thing in the World tab has one button: Place in the world, or Show in the world once it is placed. It opens the world builder with that thing selected; the World tab's own Place in the world opens it for everything. You stay where you stood while the camera flies (hold the right mouse button to look), and the camera can go anywhere, through walls too: give Director access only to people you trust.

In the world builder (where Edit takes you, and the World tab's Place in the world), Place (top left) opens the list of what you can put down in a panel down the left side, and Blueprint beside it the scenario's cards. Save (bottom right) writes the world into the scenario and saves the scenario, and you stay where you are; it says Saved (or why not), and it wears a dot while there is something to save. Exit leaves the Director; what you placed or moved since the last Save is thrown away (it asks first). The builder also saves by itself every five minutes while there is something to save, unless you turn Auto-save in the world builder off on the World tab before you go in. The hint line along the bottom says the keys: R switches the markers between moving and turning, and G turns snapping on and steps it (the hint shows the step while it is on), then off; with it off, hold Shift while dragging to snap that one drag. The selected thing's Configure opens its page on the right: who or what it is and how it behaves, the same fields as the World tab, written into the scenario as you change them, so you set it up where it stands. One you placed just now joins the scenario as you press it (Exit takes it away again with everything else placed since the last Save). The Blueprint window floats over the world: drag its head to move it, its edges and bottom corners to size it, X to close it. The grid works as it does in the Director (drag, wire, right-click to add a card). A card you pick opens its settings in the panel on the right, and what a card names lights up green in the world: its mark, and its outline where it has one. + Cards on the window's head opens the card list down the window's own left side: click a card to add it in the middle of the grid, or drag it onto the grid. Fullscreen beside it opens the full editor; its ‹ brings you back here.

Several at once: hold Ctrl and click things in the world, or rows in the Placed list, to select several (Ctrl+click one again to drop it). The markers stand in their middle, with a line, a triangle or their outline drawn through them, and move or turn them all together; the centre dot stands each one on the ground where it lands. The bubble then has Configure (one page for all of them: only what they all have, Mixed where their values differ, and what you set goes to every one; chips at its top narrow the selection to one kind), Add task (all NPCs: the task goes on the end of each list), Add to group (NPCs and props), Go to and Remove (asked first). A task added to several that goes somewhere gets one point, which they all share: each one's page says whose point it is, and Its own point gives that one a point of its own where the shared one stands. A controller and Dungeon Mode select one thing at a time.

Only once (a switch under Played again, on every card that does something and goes on): the card does its work the first time a run reaches it, and every time after the run skips it and goes straight on through its first outcome, as if it had worked. For a retry loop: a failed keypad hack texts "the guards are coming" once, not on every failed try. A card wearing it says Once on its head. Cards the run waits at for a player (prompts, skill checks, conversations, goals), flow cards and events do not have it; for a card that should stop the run the second time, use First Time Only instead.

An NPC's page has tabs along its top: General (who it is, how it behaves, its group, where it is), Outfit, Eye sight and Tasks; a car's has General, Takes and Tasks, a prop's General and Tasks. In the world builder's Configure they are the same tabs, and the one you were on stays open as you pick the next thing.

Several things on one card, and groups: most cards that name placed things take as many as you like, so one card does what several did: Car Entered goes on when any of its cars is entered, All Killed once every NPC on it is down, Show Prop puts all of its props up. Each card offers only its own kind (a car card lists cars, an NPC card NPCs). The same list offers your groups: every NPC or prop whose page gives it that Group name, as it is when the scenario plays, so an NPC added to the group later is on the card too. A group's Always present things are passed over by cards that only change what the scenario made. Talking cards, goals and the cards about one car (Give Car Key, Put in Car, Change Plate, Claim Car, Play Scripted Driving Event) still name one.

Outfit (an NPC's Outfit tab): what its ped wears in every run. The game is asked what that ped has, so only its own parts show (head, hair, upper body, legs, feet and the rest, each one it has more than one look for), each with a Style slider and, when that style comes in more than one, a Colour slider; then its accessories (hat, glasses, earrings, watch, bracelet), each from None. In the world builder its copy wears the outfit as you slide. Random picks a random one of what it has, and As the game makes it takes the outfit off again. Until you change something, it is as the game makes it; the first change keeps every part as the tab shows it. The NPC's game (the player whose game owns it) dresses it, and every other player sees what that game shows. A lore character wears their own look instead, and changing an NPC's model takes its outfit off (another ped has other clothes).

Character editor (a freemode NPC: mp_m_freemode_01 or mp_f_freemode_01): the Outfit tab's Open the character editor, or the world builder's Character editor button in the bubble beside the selected NPC, opens the same editor players make their characters in, on that NPC's look: face, heritage, hair, make-up, tattoos and clothes. You wear the look while the editor is open (the camera and the pictures work as they do for your own character), and nothing of it is saved to your character. Save puts it on the NPC (its ped becomes the look's, male or female) and takes you back to where you were, in the world builder on the NPC again when you opened it there; Cancel changes nothing. Save the scenario to keep it. With a look, the Outfit tab shows Edit its look and Take its look off instead of the clothes sliders (the look has its own clothes), and changing the NPC's model takes the look off. Every player near the NPC sees the look, face and tattoos too: each game puts it on its own copy, as it does for a lore character. It cannot open with a gun drawn or in a vehicle (it says so).

Tasks (the Tasks tab of an NPC, a car or a prop): a list of things it does, one after another, top to bottom: go to a point, wander, look at the nearest player, play an emote, get in a car and drive somewhere, set its health, die and revive; a car can speed up, freeze, sound its siren, let everyone out or blow up; a prop can slide, turn, teleport, fade and change its look. + Task lists only what that kind can do. A task that goes somewhere has a numbered point. In the world builder, Place marker puts it on the pointer and a left click puts it down where you point (Select it selects one already placed); it moves like a spot after that, every move counts at once (no Save needed for Play Tasks to use it), and the thing's points show joined by a line while it is selected. Removing a task removes its point from the world too. Play Emote plays one of /e's emotes (type it, or Choose from the emote menu: the players' menu with its pictures and videos) or, set to Animation, any animation by its dictionary and clip. Take Cover goes to its point and takes cover there, crouched behind something low or against something tall (Behind), hiding from the way its marker faces. Faces says which way it looks along its cover (left or right, as you look the way the marker faces), and it is turned that way if GTA puts it in facing the other. The next task starts as soon as it is in cover (or after a time, set so). Aim At and Shoot At use the gun it holds, else its best one, else it is handed a pistol; Shoot At sets how it shoots for its time: Accuracy, Trigger finger (40% is GTA's own pace), Fires single shots, bursts or full auto, and Fights like a rookie, a pro or a killer. A killer never holds fire: shot at, it does not duck, flinch or get pinned down, it fires as fast at a far target as a near one, it does not wait for a clear line, and from cover it keeps firing rather than peeking out now and then. It stays that way for the rest of the run, in a fight after its Shoot At too. Throw hands it what you pick (a grenade, a molotov, a smoke grenade, a flare, a snowball or a ball), throws it at a point, a placed thing or a player, and puts it away after. Revive brings it back as it was, not limping or clutching itself as GTA leaves a ped that writhed or died. Wait waits for a time, or for a card: Pick a card opens the Blueprint (in the world builder) and the next card clicked is the one; then switch on the outcomes that end the wait, any one of them (a dialog's answers, Walked away, No answer...). A Wait for a card is the run's, so an NPC a run makes waits on it; a standing one, a prop and Play Tasks pass it over. GTA Speech says one of the game's lines in the NPC's own voice or any other: Choose a voice lists every voice in the game by its ped (passers-by, gangs, jobs, the story's people), each with Hear; Line then lists only the lines that voice has, and Preview says it on the NPC in the world builder. Each task waits until it is done (it got there), or for a time you set, then the next starts; When the last one ends says whether it stops there or starts again, and an NPC's Stops to fight ends its tasks when it is attacked or has someone to fight. The run's own things play them: Spawn NPC, Spawn Car and Show Prop start them as they make the thing when Start its tasks (Start their tasks) is on, as it is by default, so no other card is needed (Check warns about a Start Tasks wired straight after one of them for the same thing: it would start them again from the top), Start Tasks starts them later, for one thing or several at once (its list offers only the NPCs, cars and props that have tasks; one a Spawn card is still making is waited for, 30 seconds at most, so they all start together from one moment: a Spawn NPC and a Spawn Car both wired into it start their tasks once, when both are done, not twice; Started then, Finished when every one of them is done, Stopped when a Stop Tasks, another Start Tasks or a Play Scripted Driving Event took them before they finished (it need not be wired: the card that took them carries on), Could not when none of them was made or none of their tasks could play; Check refuses one whose thing no card makes) and Stop Tasks stops them, leaving an NPC where it got to or sending it back to its idle. Started again from where they stopped, they pick up at the task that was playing: a teleport, a line or a throw sent with it is not done twice. A car's trailers playing their recorded tracks beside its own stop with it. Everyone sees the same thing: an NPC's and a car's tasks run on the game that owns it, which says when it has each one, and the next player's game to own it carries on from the same task; a prop's play on every game from the same moment. /npcdebug shows each NPC's and car's task, and whether its game has it. In the world builder, the Tasks tab's Play Tasks plays the list on the thing's copy where it stands while you watch from the free camera, with no test run: only on your screen, nothing is made or sent. Play with adds other things whose tasks start at the same moment (an NPC that gets in a car at the end of its take, say); it is kept with the list, and only the preview reads it. There, the nearest player is your camera (a look, an aim, a shot, a throw, a turn, running away), and a fight is not played (it is said under the button, and plays in a run). A list that starts again goes round at most once a second. Stop Tasks puts every copy back where it is placed, and so does the end of the list, a second after it ends. While a copy plays, its bubble (Configure, Remove) and its mark go along with it, and a click on it where it has got to selects it.

Takes (a car's Takes tab): drives you record, played back exactly. Record a take puts you at the wheel of a copy of the car where it is placed, its riders in their seats; the scenario's other cars wait on their own takes' starts and drive them beside you from the moment the count ends (each the take its tasks or a Play Scripted Driving Event card play, else its newest), so a race or a near miss can be timed against them, and F11 sends them back too; after 3 2 1 every frame is recorded, up to three minutes, then F10 saves it, F11 starts again from the spot and F4 throws it away (in the world builder, Record a take hands the world back to the scenario and leaves the builder first; when the take is over the builder opens again where you were, the camera where you left it and the car's Configure open). A long drive is sent packed (a three-minute one is about half a megabyte), so it can take a few seconds to save on a slow connection: the screen says how big it is while it goes. If the server is slow to answer, wait or press Save again: one drive is only ever saved once. Saved takes are listed on the car; Watch it drives a copy along it with you riding along, and Save keeps the list with the scenario. In the world builder it is Play here instead: the car's own copy drives the take, its riders in their seats, while you stay in the free camera, and the take's line is laid on the ground where it goes while the take is open and the car is selected: a white band with chevrons pointing the way the car went. Who rides in it seats NPCs from the World tab in the car. The Play Scripted Driving Event card makes the car where the take starts (and its riders, in their seats) if the run has not, and drives it exactly as recorded: speed, steering, wheel spin, brakes, lights, horn, siren, and a crash. When it is over the car brakes, everyone gets out, their own tasks start, or the driver drives on, and the card goes on through Finished. A car can also play a take as one of its tasks (Play a Scripted Driving Event). A car whose own tasks set its Lights, Indicators, Siren or Engine keeps them as those tasks set them while a take plays (in the run, on every player's screen, and in Play here): the take plays everything else it recorded. Headlights a Lights task put on stay on through a take recorded with them off. You can sit at the wheel while a take plays: the take has the engine, whether or not there is a key in it, and the vehicle dial shows its revs, its speed and the gear it was recorded in (a take recorded before takes kept the gear shows one worked out from the car's speed; record it again for the real one). The engine key does nothing until it is over. Then the car is yours as the drive left it, on the usual key rules: with a key in it the engine runs on, with none it stops. Ride along on the card does the sitting for you: the player the card is about (else the one nearest the car) is put at the wheel before the take starts, moved there behind a fade if the car is more than 30 metres away, and cannot be hurt. Only the camera, chat and the pause menu work until it is over, so you ride it as if you were driving it. An NPC the car's page seats at the wheel is not made for that card. When it ends they stay at the wheel, or get out if the ending is everyone out or their tasks start. A car the card makes for the ride has its key in the ignition, so they can drive on; one the run made already keeps its Key settings. If they cannot be seated within ten seconds, the run's log says so and the take plays without them. Every player sees it: one player's game plays all of a run's takes (the player the card is about, else the one nearest the car), is asked to keep the car while it does, and the server checks its owner the whole way through.

Trailers: a trailer is a car of the scenario like any other (the world builder's Vehicles). While you record a take, the scenario's other cars with no take of their own stand where they are placed (eight at most), so you can back the truck into a trailer and it hooks on as it does in the game; let go of it as you would in the game too. A car's Tows (its General tab) names its own trailer: place it just behind. Spawn Car then makes the trailer with the truck (unless the run has made it) and hitches it, and a recording starts with it on. Every trailer you hitch while recording is saved with the take: where it went, frame by frame, as a driving event of its own, and the moments it was hitched and let go. When the take plays (Play Scripted Driving Event, or a car's Play a Scripted Driving Event task), the trailer drives its own recorded track from the same moment on the same game, hitched and let go when it was, so it goes exactly where it went rather than wherever the game would drag it. Play Scripted Driving Event makes a trailer the run has not made where its own track starts (a car's Play a Scripted Driving Event task needs a card that made it, else the take plays without it, said in the run's log). The take's row says which trailer it has. Watch it, the world builder's Play here, and recording another car's take all drive the trailer beside the truck on its own track, so a second take can use the first one's trailer as a reference. Check says when a Tows names something that is not one of the scenario's cars, or a take's trailer is no longer placed.

Experimental recorded drives sync (/whip → Settings → Config →Vehicles, Config.ExperimentalDriveSync; off by default): a car playing a recorded drive is driven by one player's game, and everyone else sees it as the network sends it, a little late and smoothed, jumping back when an update is late on a corner. Switched on, every other player's game plays the drive itself, on a copy of the car only it has, from the same moment on the server's clock, so it is smooth and in the same place on every screen; one who comes near late starts part-way. The copy wears the car's look (paint, parts, Whiplash's stance and engine sound), with copies of the people in it and of the NPCs riding on it. The real car still drives underneath, hidden on those screens and not solid against them, so it stays the real thing for everyone: what a player does to the copy (shots, burst tyres, ramming it, hitting a rider) is done to the real car or the real NPC, and the real car's burst tyres, damage and a rider's death show on every copy. What each player sees of its state can differ a little (dents, say). When the drive ends, or the car is wrecked, or a player gets in it, the copy goes and the real car shows again.

Standing on a car: most cars throw a player off once they move (trucks and trailers do not). A car's Players and NPCs can stand on it while it moves (its General tab) keeps a player standing on it from being thrown off, on every car a run or a Test makes for it (Spawn Car, Play Scripted Driving Event). Each player's own game does it while they stand there. A very sharp turn can still slide them off, and they can jump off, be pushed or shot off as anywhere. An NPC standing on such a car rides it too: it is fixed to the car where it stands, whatever its Can move says, so the car carries it and it is never frozen in the air or put back where it was placed. It still looks, aims, shoots, plays its emote and fights from there, turning on the spot to face what it aims at, throws at or fights (and turning back to it as the car turns). A target only a few degrees off is left to its arms. A task that takes it somewhere (Go To, Walk a Route, Wander, Follow, Run Away From, Take Cover, getting in a car, Teleport), or its death, lets go of it first; standing on the car again after, it rides again. /npcdebug says riding a car.

Routes (the world builder's More, Route): points an NPC walks in turn. + Point puts the next one in front of the camera; move it like anything placed, and turn it to set the way the NPC faces while it waits there. Each point either has the NPC walk straight on (it walks on through the point to the next without stopping) or wait a number of seconds, standing, looking round, playing an emote or a scenario. Order walks them in order (back to the first, or stopping at the last), back and forth, or at random (never the same point twice in a row); Pace is a walk or a run. Finds its own way (off unless you switch it on): off, the NPC walks the straight line from each point to the next, exactly as the route is drawn; on, it takes GTA's own paths between points and goes round anything in its way, a car or a prop the run put there, the long way round if it must (good for a scene where things move). Either way, an NPC that is not on its route yet (made somewhere else, or back from a fight) finds its own way to the point first. At random the lines between points were never drawn, so it always finds its own way. In the world builder's Play Tasks the placed things are not solid, so a route that finds its own way can take a shorter path there than in a run. An NPC walks a route by its Tasks: Walk a Route goes once round it, so a list of just that set to start again is a patrol. Loosely moves each point a little either side, so two guards on one route do not walk in step, and an NPC that walks a route can always move (whatever Can move says). A standing NPC (always there, no run to start its tasks) plays its list by itself whenever it has nothing else to do: from the top the first time, and after a fight from the point nearest it. Getting in a car, fighting or shooting at players and throwing are passed over there (Check says so), and the nearest player is the nearest within 150 m. Every player sees the same patrol: it runs on the game that owns the NPC, as tasks do (/npcdebug says patrol).

Eye sight (an NPC's Eye sight tab, with Sees players on; Sees within and Cone are sliders): a guard that notices the run's players in front of it, within its distance and cone (or right beside it, whichever way it faces), with nothing in between: a wall, a car or a bush hides you, a window or a wire fence does not. A meter fills while it sees you and empties again out of sight; full, you are spotted. How long that takes depends on how far away you are: Spots you up close in (2 seconds unless you set it, never under 1) right beside it, At its full distance (8 seconds) at the edge of its range, and in proportion in between, so walking towards a guard gives you time to turn back. Sneaking (GTA's Ctrl walk) halves the distance. A spot alerts Just this guard, Its group (every NPC whose General tab has the same Group, typed as a prop's is) or Nearby NPCs that react to danger (the run's NPCs within Nearby is within, 30 m unless you set it, whose Reacts to danger is on; it is off unless you switch it on), and they Attack (they fight the run's players), Come to look (they go where you were seen, look round, then go back to their post or patrol) or do nothing by themselves (Only the card). The Guard Spots You card goes on whatever they do, with the player spotted as the one who set it off. Over the guard's head every nearby player of the run sees its mark: an eye whose ring fills as it notices you (a thin white ring when it is noticing a friend), a red ! when it has spotted someone, an amber ? while it comes to look. The server works out the cone, the distance and the meter; each player's own game only says whether something stands between that guard's eyes and them, so nobody can make a guard spot someone else. Leave the Spawn card's Fights the run's players off for a guard that sees players, so it fights only once it spots someone. In the world builder its cone lies on the ground round it while it is selected, warm near the guard and fading to its range, with the ring where it notices you whichever way it faces, the dashed arc where sneaking takes you, and the two times; it changes as you drag the sliders and type the times, and turns and moves with the guard. /npcdebug shows each player's meter.

Shipping scenarios in a resource

A resource can bring scenarios as data, no scripts: one manifest line per file. whip_core reads each when the resource starts, checks it, and offers it to a Director admin to accept. Accepted, it is a scenario like any other but read-only (Duplicate it in the editor to change it); it goes off while its resource is stopped and comes back on with it; deleting it means it is never offered again. A file that changes is offered again; what was accepted stays as it was until then.

-- fxmanifest.lua of your pack
whip_director_scenario 'scenarios/bank_job.json'
whip_director_scenario 'scenarios/drug_run.json'

Each file is a scenario document as the editor saves it ("format": 1, at most 512 KB), with "key" (its key on every server) and "requires": { "items": [...], "models": [...], "resources": [...] }. Things it ships unplaced ("coords": "spot") are placed by each server in a copy. Export as a pack (a Director admin, on a scenario in /whip) writes a scenario out in exactly this shape to whip_core/pack_exports/, with its manifest beside it.

For other resources: hearing and asking about runs

The Director tells other resources what its runs do, and answers questions about runs and scenarios (the export cards under Director runs from a script: StartScenarioRun, CanStartScenarioRun, GetScenarioRun, ListScenarioRuns, IsPlayerInScenarioRun, GetPlayerScenarioRuns, GetScenarioRunOf, GetScenario, ListScenarios, GetScenarioStats, ListDirectorCards). Two rules run through all of it:

  • A builder's Test is private. It sends no event, and every export leaves it out unless you pass { tests = true }. A script that pages its officers when a heist starts does not do it whenever someone presses Test.
  • You get copies. A run is a DirectorRunView, made when you ask: changing it changes nothing.

Settings a builder fills in for you (Settings → For scripts): its Kind (a few words, "heist, crime") and Where it happens (a placed thing: the bank, not the job giver), which are a run's and a scenario's kinds and where; and Scripts may switch it on and off (SwitchScenario).

Server eventPayload
whip_core:run:started{ run, startedBy = { mode, by } }: mode interaction · press · area · item · timer · script (by = the resource) · hand · enabled (When it's switched on: it starts as the scenario is switched on, and again after each run, with nobody in it. Its job begins as its first player joins: wait for run:playerJoined before treating it as a job going on, a heist being reported say)
whip_core:run:ended{ run, outcome, reason, vars, payout, faultCard, stopping }: outcome succeeded · failed · calledOff (a Call Off card) · aborted (an admin, the last player leaving, whip_core stopping) · faulted
whip_core:run:playerLeft{ run, source, charId, why, by, runEnds }: run is without them; sent before its run:ended; by: the resource that took them out
whip_core:run:playerJoined{ run, source, charId, by }: AddPlayerToScenarioRun
whip_core:run:signalled{ run, name, data = { value }, source }: a Send Signal card
whip_core:scenario:switchedOn / :switchedOff{ scenario, name, rev, replaced | why, by = { source, name } | { resource } | nil }: a person, a script (SwitchScenario), or the server itself

They are sent just after the Director's scheduler has done its work, so your handler never runs in the middle of a run's cards. Anything you make for a run with tag = payload.run.tag (a blip, a point, an NPC, a skill check, a car) goes when the run ends, with nothing for you to do, and anything you try to make with it after that is refused. Any server resource can fire these events too: before paying anything out on one, check GetInvokingResource() == 'whip_core' in your handler (for run:started you can also ask GetScenarioRun; an ended run is no longer there to ask).

AddEventHandler('whip_core:run:started', function(e)
    if GetInvokingResource() ~= 'whip_core' then return end
    local run = e.run
    for _, k in ipairs(run.kinds) do
        if k == 'heist' and run.where then
            -- one mark for every on-duty officer (by character: it follows them through a relog)
            local people = {}
            for _, o in ipairs(exports.whip_core:GetClockedOnEmployees('police') or {}) do
                people[#people + 1] = { charId = o.charId }
            end
            if #people > 0 then
                -- the run's tag: the mark goes when the run ends
                exports.whip_core:ShowBlip({ people = people }, 'heist:' .. run.id,
                    { coords = run.where.coords, label = 'Alarm: ' .. run.where.label, sprite = 161, color = 1, tag = run.tag })
            end
        end
    end
end)

Steering a run. A script can end a run (EndScenarioRun), put crew in or take them out (AddPlayerToScenarioRun, RemovePlayerFromScenarioRun: what the cards gave the run's players follows the crew), read and set its variables, start one with its own variables, players and places (StartScenarioRun's opts; for a scenario that starts When it's switched on, the player and opts.with join its waiting run, whose variables and places are its own already, so vars and places are refused), and switch a scenario on or off when its Settings allow it (SwitchScenario). Two cards let a builder work with a script with no card from that script: Send Signal (the script hears whip_core:run:signalled) and Wait for Script Event (the run carries on when the script calls SendDirectorEvent). A script can also put cards of its own in the palette: Cards of your own. Server scripts are trusted code: any may steer any run, and the history says which did. A builder's Test is left alone, but for EndScenarioRun.

On the player's own game (a phone's job screen, a HUD): exports.whip_core:GetMyRuns() answers the runs that player is in, { { runId, scenario, name, objective, countdown } }, and the local events whip_core:run:joined, :updated (their objective or clock changed), :left and :ended { outcome, payout } say when it changes. Only that player's runs; never a Test.

Director runs from a script

Start, read and steer the Director's scenario runs from your own resource. Building scenarios is under Director.

StartScenarioRun(key, who, opts?)SERVER

Start a run of a switched-on Director scenario for a player (who: a server id, or { charId } online): a phone app's "take the job", a job menu. Only a scenario whose Settings say A run starts: From a script, so its builder decides which ones a script may start. The player becomes its starter; Players this close join applies; one already in a run of it is refused. CanStartScenarioRun asks the same without starting one.

local runId, why = exports.whip_core:StartScenarioRun('bank_job', source)
if not runId then exports.whip_core:NotifyPlayer(source, why, 'error') end
Returns: the run's id, or false, reason (not switched on, not "From a script", already in one, its runs full)
CanStartScenarioRun(key, who)SERVER

Would StartScenarioRun start one for this player now? The same checks (switched on, "From a script" or When it's switched on with its waiting run not taken yet, on a character and up, not already in one, its runs not full), and nothing started. A phone app greys out the jobs a player cannot take, with the reason.

local ok, why = exports.whip_core:CanStartScenarioRun('bank_job', source)
ParamTypeDescription
keystringThe scenario's key
whonumber | { charId }A server id, or an online character
Returns: true, or false, reason
GetScenarioRun(runId, opts?) · ListScenarioRuns(filter?)SERVER

A Director run going now, or all of them, as a DirectorRunView: a copy made when you ask (changing it changes nothing). { id, tag, scenario, name, rev, test, kinds, where, players = { {source, charId, name} }, starter, startedAt, seconds, endsIn, vars, objectives = { {source, text, countdown} }, things = { [placedThingId] = { kind, netId, npcId, vehicleId, ... } } }. Give its tag to anything you make for the run (ShowBlip, AddPoint, SpawnNpc's opts): it goes when the run ends. A builder's Test is left out unless you pass { tests = true }.

for _, run in ipairs(exports.whip_core:ListScenarioRuns({ kind = 'heist' })) do
    print(run.name, run.where and run.where.label, #run.players)
end
ParamTypeDescription
filter.scenariostring?Runs of one scenario
filter.playernumber | { charId }?Runs a player is in
filter.kindstring?Runs of scenarios of that Kind (Settings)
filter.tests / opts.testsboolean?Include builders' Tests
Returns: GetScenarioRun: the view, or false, reason. ListScenarioRuns: a list (empty when none)
IsPlayerInScenarioRun(who, key?, opts?) · GetPlayerScenarioRuns(who, opts?)SERVER

Is a player in a run now (of that scenario, or of any), and which. who is a server id or { charId } (online).

if exports.whip_core:IsPlayerInScenarioRun(source, 'bank_job') then
    return false, 'Finish the job you are on first'
end
Returns: true | false · a list of DirectorRunViews
GetScenarioRunOf(ref, opts?)SERVER

Which run a car, an NPC or a tag belongs to: { netId }, { vehicleId }, { npcId } or { tag }. A police tracker on a getaway car, a script deciding whether a ped is part of a job.

-- A police tracker: is this car part of a heist going now?
local run = exports.whip_core:GetScenarioRunOf({ vehicleId = vehicleId })
if run then print('getaway car for', run.name) end
Returns: the run's DirectorRunView, or false, reason (not part of a run going now)
GetScenario(key) · ListScenarios(filter?)SERVER

A scenario as a DirectorScenarioView: { key, name, description, kinds, where, on, rev, draftRev, startMode, source, runs }, and from GetScenario also cards (the card types it uses), world (its placed things) and vars. It describes the revision that is switched on, or the draft when it is off. Answered from memory: it never waits. filter: { on, kind, startMode }.

Returns: the view, or false, reason · a list
GetScenarioStats(key)SERVER

How a stored scenario's runs have gone, builders' Tests left out: { runs, succeeded, stopped, lastAt } (stopped: called off, stopped by an admin, cut short). It waits on the database: call it from a thread.

CreateThread(function()   -- it waits on the database
    local stats = exports.whip_core:GetScenarioStats('bank_job')
    if stats then print(stats.runs, stats.succeeded) end
end)
Returns: the numbers, or false, reason
ListDirectorCards(filter?)SERVER

The editor's card types, each with its owner: { type, title, desc, category, inputs, outputs, labels, props, owner }. filter: { category }.

Returns: a list
StartScenarioRun(key, who, opts?) · optsSERVER

A start can say more: with (more players, as crew; 16 at most; one who is down, in the character screen or already in a run of it is left out), vars (its variables, of the types the scenario declares) and places (where THIS run's NPCs, car, items, containers and spots are: one accepted scenario, at today's gang territory). A place is { x, y, z, heading } or a vector3 / vector4 (its w the heading). Add interior = true when the place is inside an MLO: what the run makes there waits for the interior. The World tab's own "inside" is for its own spot, so a place you give is outside unless you say. A place is refused for a Standing thing (it is there before any run), a door (it is where the map has it) and a prop (its set is the scenario's).

local runId, why = exports.whip_core:StartScenarioRun('turf_war', source, {
    with = { partner },
    vars = { reward = 2500, rival = 'Ballas' },
    places = { stash = { x = 102.4, y = -1940.2, z = 20.8, heading = 90 },
               boss  = vector4(-1150.2, -1520.6, 10.6, 35.0) },
})
Returns: the run's id, or false, reason (a variable of the wrong type or one it does not have, a place it cannot take, ...)
EndScenarioRun(runId, outcome, reason?)SERVER

End a run as a card would: 'succeeded' (Succeed), 'failed' (Fail) or 'calledOff' (Call Off: no result, nobody told). Its reason carries your resource's name ('the boss is pleased (by police_mdt)', in whip_core:run:ended and its history). The one control call that also takes a builder's Test.

-- The MDT closed the case: the run fails, with your reason in its history
local ok, why = exports.whip_core:EndScenarioRun(runId, 'failed', 'the crew was arrested')
Returns: true, or false, reason
AddPlayerToScenarioRun(runId, who) · RemovePlayerFromScenarioRun(runId, who, why?)SERVER

Put a player into a run going now, or take one out. An added player is CREW: the run's doors and containers, its payouts and its items are theirs as they are the starter's. What its cards already gave "the run's players" is given to them too: the door held for the crew, the safe, its prompts and menus, its guards' targets, its goals (objective, what is left of the clock, the marks), its objective and countdown, and its blips for everyone (a blip for one player stays that player's). One taken out loses all of it. Police responding to a heist are not added: reach them with blips and notifications. Adding is refused for a Test, a player who is down or has no character, one already in a run of that scenario, and a full run (16); they are told "You joined …". Taking out gives back what the run handed them first, so RemovePlayerFromScenarioRun waits: call it from a thread. Both are announced (whip_core:run:playerJoined / :playerLeft, with by) and written into its history.

local ok, why = exports.whip_core:AddPlayerToScenarioRun(runId, friendSource)
if not ok then return false, why end

CreateThread(function()   -- taking someone out waits
    exports.whip_core:RemovePlayerFromScenarioRun(runId, friendSource, 'left the crew')
end)
Returns: true, or false, reason
GetScenarioRunVar(runId, name) · SetScenarioRunVar(runId, name, value)SERVER

A run's variable, read or set. Set takes the type the scenario declares it (number, text, true/false). Get answers true, value (true first: a variable can hold false or nothing) or false, reason. Cards read a variable when they reach it, so a value you set is seen by the next card that reads it. Not written into the history.

local ok, score = exports.whip_core:GetScenarioRunVar(runId, 'score')
if ok then
    exports.whip_core:SetScenarioRunVar(runId, 'score', (score or 0) + 10)
end
Returns: Get: true, value, or false, reason. Set: true, or false, reason
SendDirectorEvent(name, payload?, opts?)SERVER

Tell runs something: every Wait for Script Event card waiting for name carries on (a builder types the name on the card). name is in your namespace, 'police.backupArrived': the first running resource to send in a namespace has it until it stops, another is refused with its name, and whip_core's own (npc., player. ... ) are nobody's. payload.source (a server id) is who it is about: the card's "About a player in this run" waits for one of its players, and what follows acts for them. opts.runId: only that run hears it. An event about none of its players goes on for whoever the card's branch was for. At most 20 of one event a second, and 60 a second from one resource whatever their names ("too often"). A builder's Test never hears a real script's event, and its run id is no run a script can name. To try a Wait card in your Test, /director send <event> [value] (any Director builder) puts the event into your own Test, about you.

-- an officer pressed "en route" on the MDT (checked in your own SecureEvent first)
local ok, heard = exports.whip_core:SendDirectorEvent('police.backupArrived', { source = robber, unit = 'Adam-12' })
Returns: true, heardBy (how many runs heard it), or false, reason
SwitchScenario(key, on, why?)SERVER

Switch a scenario on or off by script: heists only at night. on is true or false. Only one whose Settings say Scripts may switch it on and off; on again only at the revision a person last switched on (never a draft nobody did, never one a person switched off); never while a builder tests it. Off calls off every run of it going now, with your reason and your resource's name ('daytime (switched off by heist_clock)'). Off while it is already off in the world but meant to be on (its pack restarting, the server starting) is remembered, so it does not come back on behind you. In memory only: a reboot puts back what a person chose, and a person switching it (/whip, /director on / stop) forgets yours. whip_core:scenario:switchedOn / :switchedOff say by = { resource = 'your_resource' }, and /whip says "On · by your_resource" / "Off · by your_resource". It reads the revision, so it waits: call it from a thread.

-- Heists only at night: look at the clock once a minute, switch when night starts or ends
CreateThread(function()
    local wasNight
    while true do
        local hour = exports.whip_core:GetTime()
        local night = hour >= 22 or hour < 5
        if night ~= wasNight then
            exports.whip_core:SwitchScenario('bank_job', night, 'night only')
            wasNight = night
        end
        Wait(60000)
    end
end)
Returns: true, or false, reason

Director: cards of your own

A resource can put cards of its own in the Director's palette, and builders drag them into scenarios like whip_core's own. Your code stays in your resource: whip_core gets the card as data and runs your functions through whip's helper (@whip_core/lib/satellite.lua), so a mistake in them reaches the console in its own words.

A minigame does not need a card of its own: add it as a skill check game and it is a choice in the Skill Check card's Game field, with that card's outcomes (Passed, Missed, and Couldn't start for a player who lacks what it needs: wire that one back to the card before, a Wait for Press, so they can try again). Running out of time is a miss, and so is a game that never answers (it froze, or lost the server). whip_phone's seven phone games come in that way.

Whip.card(type, def)SERVER

Add a card, or change one. type is '<your namespace>.<name>': the first running resource to use a namespace has it, for its cards and its events (SendDirectorEvent). Call it at file scope or inside Whip.register: it is sent again whenever whip_core restarts. A refusal is printed in your console with the reason.

FieldTypeDescription
titlestringThe card's name in the palette
desc, helpstring?One line under it, and the longer help the editor shows
category, categoryTitle, color, iconstring?Its palette group (default: your namespace) and that group's name; a colour (blue, teal, green, amber, red, violet, slate); an icon
outputsstring[]Its outcomes, one pin each. labels = { sent = 'Sent' } names them; bad lists the ones drawn as going wrong
propstable[]?Its fields (up to 40), each { key, kind, label, default?, required?, hint?, unit?, group?, showIf? }. group (up to 30 characters) puts a heading over that field and the ones after it, for a card with many fields. showIf names one of the card's bool fields: the field shows only while that switch is on. kind: text (maxLength, lines 1–6), number or duration (min, max), bool, select (up to 200 options: text, or { value, label }), world (a placed thing; worldKind: 'spot', 'npc', 'vehicle'…), item, var, job, players, lore, entries (a list on the card that one of your Director buttons fills: button its id, a button for kind 'card'; add the words to add one; max 1–12. Each entry is plain data, its text shown on its row; your run gets the list)
runfunction(card)?Its code, and it may wait. Return an outcome, or nothing and answer later with Whip.answerCard. card is below
instantboolean?It answers at once and never waits
timeoutnumber?Seconds before Took Too Long (30; the builder can change it)
eventtable?{ name, match = 'player' | 'run' | 'any', once?, filter? } in place of run: the card goes on when you send that event (SendDirectorEvent)
failtable?A Fail Condition of your own, in place of run and outputs: { event, match?, ends?, reason?, filter? }. Wired to nothing, it watches the whole run, and when you send event (SendDirectorEvent, source one of its players) the run fails for everyone, or only that player is taken out. It gets the Fail Conditions' own fields: When it is broken (ends: 'everyone' or 'them', its default) and Why (reason, its default). match as an event card's ('player' by default). filter(card, event), when given: true or the words to tell them breaks it, false or nil not this time. It shows with whip_core's Fail Conditions
checkfunction(props, doc)?A problem the editor shows: return a message, and 'warning' for one that does not stop a run. doc holds the scenario's vars, its world ({ id, kind, label } each) and data[worldId], what your own buttons saved on each thing
onEndfunction(callId, why)?It ended without your answer (it took too long, its run ended): tidy up what it made
testSaysstring?What a builder's Test says in place of running your code; {message} fills in a field
test'run'?Your code runs in a builder's Test too, with card.test true: keep what it does to card.player
permissionstring?Only people with this permission may add it or change its fields
v, renamednumber?, table?Bumped when its fields change; what it was called before, { ['old.type'] = { pins = { old = 'new' } } }
once, onceOutboolean?, string?Every card with an outcome gets an Only once switch: set, it does its work the first time a run reaches it, and every time after the run skips it and goes straight on through onceOut (its first outcome when left out). once = false leaves the switch off a card the run waits at for a player (a prompt, a choice)
Whip.card('mycafe.callStaff', {
    title = 'Call Staff', color = 'teal',
    desc = 'Tells the café staff on duty, with a message.',
    outputs = { 'sent', 'nobody' }, labels = { sent = 'Sent', nobody = 'Nobody on duty' }, bad = { 'nobody' },
    props = { { key = 'message', kind = 'text', label = 'Message', default = 'A customer is waiting', maxLength = 120 } },
    testSays = 'Would send "{message}" to the staff on duty',
    run = function(card)
        local staff = Whip.call('GetClockedOnEmployees', 'mycafe')
        if type(staff) ~= 'table' or #staff == 0 then return 'nobody' end
        for _, s in ipairs(staff) do
            if s.source then Whip.call('NotifyPlayer', s.source, card.props.message, 'info') end
        end
        card:record('called', { detail = card.props.message })
        return 'sent'
    end,
})
Returns: true, or false (printed) when def is not a card
card: what your run is handedSERVER

A copy of what the card is doing, with methods that call back into whip_core. The methods are refused once the card has finished. Give card.tag to anything you make for the run (ShowBlip, AddPoint): it goes when the run ends.

Field or methodDescription
callId, runId, cardIdThis call, its run and the card in the scenario. callId answers it later: never send it to a player's game
scenario, name, rev, tag, testThe scenario's key, name and revision; the run's tag; true in a builder's Test
player, starter, players, trigger, propsWho the run acts for now, who started it, its players (server ids), what started it, and the card's fields as the builder set them, but for two kinds, which arrive ready to use: a world field is the placed thing, { id, kind, label, coords = { x, y, z }, heading } (nil when nothing is placed), and a players field is a list of server ids (everyone in the run, the starter, or the one player the card is for)
card:var(name) · card:setVar(name, value)The run's variables
card:state() · card:setState(t)This card's own state, kept between its calls
card:place(id) · card:made(id)A placed thing's place, and what the run made for it
card:record(kind, { source?, detail? })A line in the run's history
card:objective(text, { who? }) · card:clearObjective()The players' objective band. It comes down by itself when the card ends without your answer (Took Too Long, Didn't Work, the run ended); when you answer, take it down first if it should go
card:clock(seconds, label)A countdown on the band (0 stops it), taken down the same way
card:give(src, item, n, metadata?)Items for the run, as Give Item gives them: the player's to keep in a live run; a Test takes them back when it ends
card:pay(src, amount, { method?, reason? }) · card:charge(src, amount, { method?, reason? })Money, with the run's protections: in a Test, Pay only says it and Charge charges nothing
card:finish('succeeded' | 'failed' | 'calledOff', reason?)Ends the run
card:log(fmt, …)A line in the server console, naming the run and the card
Returns: var, state, place and made answer the value, or nil, why; the rest true, or false, why
Whip.answerCard(callId, outcome, data?) · AnswerDirectorCardSERVER

Answer a card later, from anywhere: an officer pressing E at the place, a phone reply. outcome is one of the card's own; data.source is which of the run's players what follows acts for. Only the resource whose card it is may answer it, and only while it still waits.

A wrong outcome does not retry the card. An outcome the card does not have (a typo, 'timeout', 'didntWork') ends the card as Didn't Work, or stops the run with the reason when nothing is wired to Didn't Work, and answers false, reason. The card is no longer waiting, so a second answer is refused too.
Whip.answerCard(callId, 'responded', { source = officer })
Returns: true, or false, reason (it is no longer waiting, or the outcome is not one of its own)
Whip.removeCard(type) · Whip.scenario(key, doc) · Whip.template(name, doc)SERVER

Whip.removeCard takes one of your cards away (they all go by themselves when your resource stops). Whip.scenario offers a scenario built in code to the server's Director admins: pending until one accepts it, unless they trust your resource, then read-only there. Whip.template adds a starting point to the editor's New list, and a builder's copy of it is theirs. doc is a scenario document as the editor saves it. Both are sent again whenever whip_core restarts, and the same one again changes nothing.

Returns: removeCard: true, or false, reason. scenario, template: nothing (a refusal is printed)
TestDirectorCard(type, props?, opts)SERVER

Run one of your cards once without the editor, as a builder's Test is, for a player: its real code runs, with card.test true, so keep what it does to card.player. Give hands out what the run's end takes back, Pay only says it, Charge charges nothing, and no script hears of the run. It waits until the card answers: call it from a thread.

ParamTypeDescription
typestringOne of your own cards
propstable?Its fields, as the editor sets them; a place field takes { x, y, z, heading? }
opts.playernumberWhose test run it is (required)
opts.secondsnumber?How long to wait, 1 to 120 (default: its Give up after, and 5 more)
opts.eventtable?An event card's payload, as SendDirectorEvent's
RegisterCommand('testcall', function(source)
    CreateThread(function()   -- it waits: a thread, and Whip.call answers if whip_core stops meanwhile
        local result, why = Whip.call('TestDirectorCard', 'mycafe.callStaff', { message = 'Test call' }, { player = source })
        print(result and result.outcome or why)
    end)
end, true)
Returns: { outcome, data } ('timeout' when its time ran out), or false, reason (Check's first problem, it failed, it did not answer in time)
TestDirectorScenario(doc, opts) · SteerDirectorTest(runId, op, ...) · GetDirectorTestResult(runId)SERVER

Run a whole scenario document once as a Test for a player, the way the editor's Test runs it, and steer it the way the test map does: take an outcome of a waiting card, give an answer to a talk, send an event, set a variable, end it. Nothing of value is kept: Give hands out what the run's end takes back, Pay and Charge only say what they would do, and no script hears of the run. It must pass Check (a run that can never succeed is tested all the same). One per player at a time, and three of yours at a time. It waits until the run ends: call it from a thread, or pass wait = false and steer it as it goes.

ParamTypeDescription
doctableA scenario document, as the editor saves it
opts.playernumberWhose test run it is (required, on a character)
opts.secondsnumber?1 to 600 (default 60): still going then, it is ended (late)
opts.varstable?{ name = value }, set before its first card plays
opts.steertable?Done in order: { op = 'take', node, pin } and { op = 'say', node, option, amount? } once their card waits; 'event', 'emit' and 'var' at once or once their when card waits; { op = 'end' }; { op = 'wait', ms }
opts.waitboolean?false: answer at once, still running

SteerDirectorTest does one of the same ops now, on a test of yours that is still going: 'take', nodeId, pin, 'say', nodeId, option, amount?, 'event', name, payload? (a script's event), 'emit', name, payload? (one of the Director's own, to this run alone), 'var', name, value, 'end', outcome?, reason?. GetDirectorTestResult reads one of yours, going or ended (kept ten minutes after its end).

CreateThread(function()
    local r = exports.whip_core:TestDirectorScenario(doc, { player = source, steer = {
        { op = 'say', node = 'offer', option = 'opt1' },   -- answer 1 of the Dialog Line 'offer'
    } })
    print(r and r.status, r and r.reason)
end)
Returns: a result: { runId, status, reason, vars, steps, fired, entered, waiting, things, done, late }; fired[card][outcome] counts each way it went. Or false, reason (it could not start). SteerDirectorTest: true, or false, reason.

Director: tasks and buttons of your own

Besides cards, a resource can add three more things to the Director. Tasks go in the Tasks list of NPCs and cars, next to Go To and Play a Scripted Driving Event. Buttons belong to one kind of placed thing: they show on that thing's page and in the world builder's bubble beside it, never on the screen by themselves. A button can keep data of its own on the thing, saved with the scenario, and a run hands that data back to your server side when it makes the thing. Weapons of your own (add-on weapons you stream) join GTA's in every weapon list. Your namespace is the same one your cards use. Everything you add goes away by itself when your resource stops.

Example: a tuning resource adds a Customise button for cars. It opens its own tuning screen on the placed car and saves the chosen paint and parts on it. When a run spawns that car, the resource hears whip_core:run:thingMade and applies them. It can also add a Fit a Part task that a scenario's car plays partway through a run, and a Car Is Tuned card (Whip.card) that checks it.

Whip.task(type, def)SERVER CLIENT

Add a task, or change one. Call it once, in a file that both sides load: the server sends the task to the editor as data, and every game keeps your run, which plays the step on the game that owns the NPC or car. That game changes as players move about, and the new owner runs a timed or lasting step again from its start, so keep run to what the entity itself does. The world builder's Play here runs it on its own copy, with info.preview set.

FieldTypeDescription
labelstringIts name in the + Task picker (40 letters at most)
descstring?One line about what it does
groupstring?The picker's group: one of the Director's (move, look, fight, act, car, body, wait) or one of your own, named by groupTitle. Default: your namespace
kindsstring[]Who can do it: 'npc', 'vehicle'. A prop's tasks are whip_core's only
timingstring?'instant' (done once it has started), 'timed' (lasts sec seconds: the default), 'until' (until it is done, giving up after giveUp seconds), 'either' (the builder picks; next = 'done' or 'time' is the default)
secnumber?A timed step's length in seconds (3). The builder can change it per step
giveUpnumber?An until step's limit in seconds (30). The builder can change it per step
lastingboolean?It keeps going after its slot: a Wait after it keeps the thing at it
onceboolean?A new owner never plays it again (it would happen twice: a line of speech, a throw)
standingboolean?false: a standing NPC passes it over (it needs a run)
fieldstable[]?Up to 8, each { key, kind, label, hint?, default?, required? }. Kinds: number (min, max, unit; slider = true with a step draws it as a slider and needs min and max), bool, select (1 to 200 options; look = 'seg' draws 2 to 4 of them as a row of buttons), text (max), world (one of the scenario's placed things; worldKind limits it), point (key 'at': a place the world builder puts down), target (key 'target': the nearest player, who set the card off, a placed thing or a point)
runfunctionrun(entity, args, info), on the game that owns the thing, in a thread of its own (it may wait). args are the fields: a world field is that thing's entity on this game (nil when it is not here), a target is { kind, entity, coords }, a point { x, y, z, heading }. info is { type, kind, timing, ms, preview }
donefunction?An until step's check, asked every quarter second: true is done, 'failed' failed, anything else not yet. Without it, the step is done when run returns (false or an error: failed)
-- shared/director.lua, in shared_scripts
Whip.task('mycafe.flash', {
    label = 'Flash the Lights', group = 'car', kinds = { 'vehicle' }, timing = 'timed', sec = 4,
    fields = { { key = 'times', kind = 'number', label = 'Times', min = 1, max = 20, default = 5 } },
    run = function(car, args)
        for _ = 1, args.times do
            SetVehicleLights(car, 2) Wait(200)
            SetVehicleLights(car, 1) Wait(200)
        end
        SetVehicleLights(car, 0)
    end,
})
Returns: true, or false when it is not a task (printed). whip_core's own answer is printed when it refuses one. Whip.removeTask(type) takes one away on the side it is called on.
Whip.weapons(list, opts)SERVER CLIENT

Offer your own add-on weapons (the WEAPON_* names in your weapons.meta) beside GTA's, everywhere whip lists weapons: an NPC's Weapon on the Director's World tab, the Hold a Weapon task, the world builder's More, Weapons (a firearm with a world model becomes a Fixed Weapon), Dungeon Mode, and the Object Viewer's Give a weapon. Each shows with your tag after it, so Pump Shotgun (gunny) sits next to GTA's own Pump Shotgun. Call it once, in a file that both sides load: the server's list decides what Check and a run accept, each game's what its editor offers (only the weapons that game has). Calling it again replaces your list.

A scenario that uses one of your weapons waits for it when the server starts: it comes back on by itself once your resource has added it. While your resource is stopped, Check says the weapon comes from it. An NPC given one of your weapons carries the gun itself, never your item, so your own ammo and reload code is not on it.

FieldTypeDescription
list[n].namestringThe weapon's name: WEAPON_ and capitals, digits or _ (64 at most). Never one of GTA's own
list[n].labelstringIts name in the lists (40 letters at most)
list[n].groupstringpistol, smg, rifle, machine gun, shotgun, sniper, heavy, thrown, stun gun or melee
list[n].modelstring?A firearm's world model (its <Model>): with one it can be a Fixed Weapon. Never one of GTA's models
opts.tagstring?What shows after each label (16 letters at most). Default: your resource's name
-- config/weapon_catalog.lua, in shared_scripts
Whip.weapons({
    { name = 'WEAPON_MY_PUMP', label = 'Pump Shotgun', group = 'shotgun', model = 'w_sg_my_pump' },
    { name = 'WEAPON_MY_KNIFE', label = 'Knife', group = 'melee' },
}, { tag = 'mine' })
Returns: true, or false when it is not a list (printed). whip_core's own answer is printed when it refuses one, and then none of the list is added. Whip.removeWeapons() takes yours away on the side it is called on.
Whip.directorButton(id, def)CLIENT

Add a button for a kind of placed thing, or change one. It shows under Tools on the thing's page (in the editor and in the world builder's Configure panel), in a row under the world builder's bubble when the thing is selected, or in both. Pressed, your press runs on that player's game, in a thread of its own, handed the thing. A thing put down in the world builder but not in the scenario yet is added to it first, as Configure does.

FieldTypeDescription
labelstringThe button's text (24 letters at most)
kindsstring[]Which placed things have it: npc, vehicle, prop, spot, groundItem, container, door, route
wherestring?'page', 'bubble' or 'both' (the default)
takesOverboolean?The Director steps out of the way first, as recording a take does: the world builder hands back what it has, the page hides, the mouse is let go. You have the screen until you call thing:back(); then the Director comes back, the world builder open on the thing again. If your code throws, or your resource stops, it comes back by itself
iconstring?One of whip's icons by its key, as AddAction's ('turbo', 'lock')
hintstring?Its tooltip
pressfunctionpress(thing). thing is { id, kind, label, model, models, coords, scenario, data, entity, builder }: data is what you keep on it, entity the world builder's copy while it is open (never for a button that takes over), builder whether it was pressed there. A random vehicle (the world builder's first Vehicles tile) has models, every model a run picks from, and is pressed for one of them: model (each model on its page has your button). A button for kind 'card' fills your card's entries field: its thing is the card, with card = { type, field, entry, value, props, world } (entry the one being changed, nil for a new one; world the card's placed things by field), and thing:save(t) keeps t as that entry

thing:save(t) keeps t on the thing: plain data, 4 KB of JSON at most, nil takes it away. It is an edit of the open scenario like any other, so Save keeps it and Ctrl+Z undoes it. thing:back(t?) hands the screen back after a button that takes over, keeping t first when given.

-- client.lua
Whip.directorButton('mycafe.customise', {
    label = 'Customise', icon = 'turbo', kinds = { 'vehicle' }, takesOver = true,
    press = function(thing)
        local paint = OpenMyTuningScreen(thing.model, thing.coords, thing.data)   -- yours; waits until it closes
        thing:back(paint and { paint = paint } or nil)
    end,
})
Returns: true, or false when it is not a button (printed). Whip.removeDirectorButton(id) takes one away. thing:save and thing:back: true, or false, reason
Whip.objectViewerOption(id, def)CLIENT

An option of yours in the object viewer's list (the /w developer tool: G on what it has picked out opens its options down the right of the screen), from @whip_core/lib/satellite.lua. Shown for the kinds you name, and for whip's own things only (whip = true: a saved car, a player), the game's only (false: a street car, an NPC walking by), or both (left out). id is '<your namespace>.<name>'; called again, it changes the option; it goes when your resource stops. Shown only to someone with dev tools on, but anything select does on the server checks for itself (HasDevTools).

Whip.objectViewerOption('autos.whiplash', {
    label = 'Open Whiplash', group = 'Whiplash', tint = 'violet',
    hint  = 'Takes the driver\'s seat and opens the shop on this car.',
    kinds = { 'vehicle' }, whip = true,
    select = function(target)   -- { kind, entity, netId, whip, vehicleId, serverId, model, name, coords }
        TriggerServerEvent('my_autos:open', target.netId)
    end,
})
Returns: true, or false (printed). tint: blue, teal, green, amber, red, violet or slate. Whip.removeObjectViewerOption(id) takes one away
GetDirectorThingData(where, worldId)SERVER

What your buttons saved on a placed thing: a copy. where is a run's id (that run's revision of the scenario) or a scenario's key (the revision that is on now). The same data comes two other ways. A card of yours reads it with card:made(id).data. The event whip_core:run:thingMade fires each time a run makes something for one of its placed things: { run, world, kind, label, netId, npcId, vehicleId, containerId, groundId, doorId, data }, where data[GetCurrentResourceName()] is yours. It fires in a builder's Test too (run.test is true), since what you keep on a thing is often how it comes out (Whiplash's look on a car), and a Test must show that; check run.test if yours must not act on one. An Always present thing fires it when the scenario is switched on (or a Test starts), with no run: { scenario, standing = true, test, world, kind, ... }. netId may be nil for a moment after a car is made.

AddEventHandler('whip_core:run:thingMade', function(e)
    if GetInvokingResource() ~= 'whip_core' then return end
    local mine = e.data[GetCurrentResourceName()]
    if e.kind == 'vehicle' and mine and mine.paint then PaintRunCar(e.vehicleId, mine.paint) end   -- yours
end)
Returns: a table, nil (nothing saved), or false, reason (no such run, scenario or thing)

Voice: keys, items, settings

whip_voice is whip's voice system. The people near you hear you in 3D, muffled through walls and doors, heard from the doorway or window between you, and different in cars and underwater. A phone call carries the phone's full sound, and on speaker it works both ways: the other side hears the people near the phone too. The radio is clear up close, then breaks up with static in the gaps and fades out by its range. Voice is private, because the server decides who hears whom and a modified game cannot change that. whip_phone's calls, the radio and megaphone items, the HUD's voice light and your own resources (For other resources) all go through it. It runs its own voice server on the same machine as your FiveM server: nothing to install, only one line in server.cfg (WHIP's recipe writes it) and the voice ports open (Setting up whip_voice).

Keys

Players can change these in GTA's Settings > Key Bindings > FiveM. The ones below are the defaults.

KeyBindingWhat it does
NVoice: push to talkTalk to the people near you. The HUD's voice circle lights blue.
Caps LockVoice: radio push to talkTalk on your radio (while it is on). The circle goes orange with a radio. The people next to you still hear you too.
ZCycle Voice RangeWhisper (3 m), normal (8 m), shout (20 m), whip_core's key.
LB + A · LB + XA controller's talk and radioHeld, as the keys. Players move them on the pause menu's Controller screen.

Items

ItemUse it
megaphoneHold it up (an animation, the megaphone in hand): your voice carries 6 times as far and sounds like a bullhorn. Use it again to put it away, or it goes down by itself if you get in a car, draw a weapon, drop it or die.
radioA 3D handheld radio comes up in the bottom right of the screen, worked with the mouse: click the right knob for power and drag or scroll it for volume; the middle knob is the channel, 100 to 999 (or the ▲ ▼ keys, or type it and press #). The channel is the frequency. While it is on, everyone on the same frequency hears you on Caps Lock (or while you hold the bar on its side): clear up to 500 m apart, then cutting out with bursts of static (more often the further), garbled, and fading away to nothing by 1.5 km. Esc puts it away; it keeps working. It turns off if you lose the radio. While you are down it stays on and you still hear it, but you cannot talk on it, open it or change it.
On a controller (its buttons show beside the radio): A power, D-pad up / down the channel (hold it and it runs, ten at a time after a moment), D-pad left / right the volume, RB held to talk, X the speaker, Y key beeps on or off, B or Start puts it away. You stand still while it is up, on a controller as on a keyboard.
radio on speakerThe grey button on top of the radio: the people standing near you hear what comes out of your radio too, from where you stand, like a phone on speaker. It is not louder for you. It goes off with the radio. Someone whose own radio is on the same frequency hears it on their own radio only, never twice.
whip_voice registers these items. Give them like any item: exports.whip_core:AddItem(source, 'radio', 1).

Commands

CommandWhoWhat
/voicecheckdeveloper mode, consoleChecks voice from the game's side, and says what to fix: the voice system, the voice server (and Windows Firewall, for the built-in one), and every player's game (connected, over UDP or TCP, and whether it can read the secret). See Setting up whip_voice.
/voicestatusdeveloper mode, consolewhip_voice's state: the voice address, the room, and each player connected, with how many voices they hear.
/voicevolume 0-200everyoneHow loud the people around you are (100 is normal, 0 mutes them). Calls and the radio have their own volumes. Kept on your PC.
/voicedebugdeveloper modeShows what each voice goes through (muffled by what, heard from which doorway) and every door and window of the building you're in.

Each player's own voice settings, in the pause menu's Server Settings (Chat & voice), kept on their PC:

SettingWhat it is
Voice volumeHow loud the people around you are (/voicevolume too).
Phone call volumeHow loud the other side of a call is. The same setting as the phone's Settings > Sounds > Call volume: change one and the other follows.
Radio volumeHow loud the radio is. Its own volume knob changes it too.
Background noise suppressionA switch: takes fans, keyboards and background hum out of your microphone before anyone hears it. On unless the server's Config.Quality.noiseSuppression says otherwise. It changes at once, without leaving voice; you are silent for the moment it takes.

Settings worth knowing (whip_voice/config.lua)

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
Config.Ranges3 / 8 / 20How far whisper, normal and shout carry, in metres.
Config.FullVolumeWithin1.0Full volume only this close (in your face); from there a voice fades steadily over its whole range to silence at the edge.
Config.SideSeparation6How much quieter someone on your left is in your right ear (and the other way round), on top of the 3D, in dB: 0 the 3D alone, 12 strong.
Config.Environment.headphone3DtrueFull 3D made for headphones. false for plain left/right panning, if voices sound hollow or boxy.
Config.MaxVoices100The most voices one player is connected to at once (the nearest). Only matters in a crowd bigger than this.
Config.Megaphone.rangeMultiplier6How many times further a megaphone voice carries (normal 8 m becomes 48 m).
Config.Megaphone.carMuffle4How many dB a closed car takes off a megaphone voice (a normal voice: Config.Muffle.car, 9). A bullhorn is loud, so it gets through, dulled.
Config.RadioCaps Lock, 500 / 1500 m, 100-999The radio's key, how far it is clear, how far it reaches, its frequencies.
Config.Radio.staticVolume0.06How loud the static is when a weak radio voice cuts out (0 none, 1 very loud). It only plays in the gaps, never over the voice.
Config.Radio.distortion1.0How garbled a weak radio voice sounds as it breaks up: thinner, clipped and gritty (0 clean, 1 normal, 1.5 the most).
Config.Radio.speakerRange8How far, in metres, the people around you hear your radio on speaker (8 is as far as a normal voice).
Config.Radio.uiSoundstrueThe 3D radio's key and power beeps. false for none. The talk beeps stay either way: a short beep as someone starts talking on the radio and the two-tone roger beep as they stop, heard by them and by everyone on the frequency.
Config.Quality.bitrateKbps64Voice quality (Discord uses 64).
Config.Quality.noiseSuppressiontrueBackground noise suppression for players who have not chosen. Each player can switch it in Server Settings.
Config.CrowdQuality40 → 40 kbps, 80 → 24 kbpsVoices heard by big crowds send less, so a crowd does not swamp the voice server.
Config.Quality.silentWhenQuietfalseSend nothing at all while the key is up. Saves a little on huge crowds; the first word of each press comes ~30 ms later.

Setting up whip_voice

For server owners. Nothing to install: whip_voice brings its own voice server (LiveKit) and runs it on the same machine as your FiveM server. One line in server.cfg and the voice ports open, and it works.

What you need

  • FXServer on Windows or Linux (64-bit), on a machine whose ports you can open: a VPS, a dedicated server, or your own PC. Rented FiveM hosting with only a control panel works if the host lets you open the voice ports; if it cannot, use a voice server of your own somewhere else.
  • This line in server.cfg, above ensure whip_voice. WHIP's txAdmin recipe writes it for you. FXServer lets a resource start a program only with it, and the voice server is a program. ("Unsafe" is FXServer's word for any resource allowed to: whip_voice starts the voice server and the voice bot, and Windows' own tar and PowerShell to unpack them and read the firewall, nothing else.) Without it, the console says so, with the line to add.
  • The voice ports open, inbound (below): players' games send their voices to them, as they join through 30120.
add_unsafe_child_process_permission whip_voice

That is all: no domain name, no certificate, no service to install, no keys to copy. The signalling (who joins, who hears whom) goes through your FiveM server's own connection with each player; only the voices themselves go to the voice ports.

Opening the voice ports

UDP 7882 to 7893   voices
TCP 7881           voices, when a player's network blocks UDP
  • Windows Firewall. The first time the voice server starts, Windows may ask whether to let livekit-server.exe through: click Allow (on a server, tick Public networks too). Or double-click resources\whip_voice\service\Open voice ports.bat: it asks for administrator rights and opens the ports. On a server nobody is logged into, that is the way, as no box comes up there. If someone clicked Cancel, Windows blocks the voice server whatever the ports say: the same file takes the block away. When the FiveM server itself runs as administrator, whip_voice opens the ports at start by itself. Nothing to restart either way.
  • Your host's firewall. Some hosts have one of their own in their website's control panel (OVH, Hetzner, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud). Allow the ports there, as you did 30120.
  • At home, behind a router: forward them to this machine, as you did 30120. Linux with ufw: ufw allow 7882:7893/udp and ufw allow 7881/tcp.

The first start

whip_voice downloads the voice server (about 20 MB) into whip_voice\bin, checks it is the genuine file, starts it with new random keys (they are never written to disk) and opens the voice room. The voice bot, which plays recorded lines into phone calls as the Director's lore characters (Lore phone calls), comes in the background: its own copy of Node.js and its packages, about 100 MB, then it starts. Voice works meanwhile. Both start and stop with the FiveM server, and one that stops by itself is started again. The console says each step:

[whip_voice] built-in voice server: downloading LiveKit 1.13.7, the voice server (once, about 20 MB)...
[whip_voice] built-in voice server: LiveKit 1.13.7 is running. Players' games send voices to UDP 7882-7893 ...
[whip_voice] voice room whipvoice-6fd35ef1 open
[whip_voice] voice bot: running (lore characters can phone players)

Later starts download nothing. Updating whip_voice by replacing its folder takes bin with it, so the next start downloads them again. whip_voice\bin\logs keeps the voice server's and the bot's logs. The first time each player joins, FiveM asks them to allow the microphone: its box takes the mouse only with the F8 console open.

Checking it

/voicecheck, in game with developer mode on (or voicecheck in txAdmin's Live Console), checks the voice server, Windows Firewall, every player's game (connected, over UDP or TCP, with a microphone) and the voice bot. It says OK, or what is wrong and how to fix it, top to bottom: an early problem often causes the later ones. voicestatus in the console shows who is connected and what each player picks up.

Settings

All optional, in server.cfg with plain set, before ensure whip_voice:

SettingWhat it isDefault
whip_voice_udpThe UDP ports for voices: one (7882) or a range.7882-7893
whip_voice_tcpThe TCP port for players whose network blocks UDP.7881
whip_voice_ipThe public IPv4 players' games send voices to.found by asking the internet
whip_voice_apiWhere the voice server listens for this FiveM server, on this machine only.http://127.0.0.1:7880
whip_voice_botfalse: no voice bot (lore characters cannot phone players).on
whip_voicebot_urlWhere the voice bot listens, on this machine only.http://127.0.0.1:7899

The voice bot's own settings (calls at once, the sites recordings may come from, how long and big they may be) are Config.VoiceBot in whip_voice's config.lua. Two FiveM servers on one machine (Legacy and Enhanced) each run a voice server of their own, so the second needs other ports, open as well: whip_voice_udp "7982-7993", whip_voice_tcp "7981", whip_voice_api "http://127.0.0.1:7980" and whip_voicebot_url "http://127.0.0.1:7999". For Windows Firewall, run "Open voice ports.bat" -Udp 7982-7993 -Tcp 7981 from a command prompt in whip_voice\service.

What the problems mean

It saysWhat it meansWhat to do
FXServer lets a resource start programs only when server.cfg allows itserver.cfg has no add_unsafe_child_process_permission whip_voice.Add the line above ensure whip_voice, and restart the server.
Windows Firewall BLOCKS the voice serverSomeone clicked Cancel when Windows asked about livekit-server.exe.Double-click whip_voice\service\Open voice ports.bat.
Windows Firewall: the voice ports are not open yet, or does not let voices inNo rule lets them in yet.Click Allow when Windows asks, or double-click Open voice ports.bat.
all players connect over TCPUDP 7882-7893 is not getting through.Allow UDP 7882-7893 inbound in the host's firewall (and Windows Firewall).
(everyone) is not connected to voiceThe voice ports are shut.Open UDP 7882-7893 and TCP 7881, in Windows Firewall and the host's.
some players connect over TCPTheir own network blocks UDP.Nothing on your side. Voice works for them, but can stutter.
something already answers on 127.0.0.1:7880Another voice server is there: the setup wizard's "LiveKit" service, say.Use it (keep the wizard's lines in server.cfg), uninstall it ("Setup voice server.bat" -Uninstall), or give the built-in one other ports (Settings).
… does not match its published checksum, answered 403, or could not unpackThe download was cut off or changed on the way, or the machine cannot reach github.com.Restart whip_voice to try again. The machine needs HTTPS to github.com (and nodejs.org and registry.npmjs.org, for the bot).
the voice server stopped five times in a rowIt cannot run, often because another program holds one of its ports.whip_voice\bin\logs\livekit.log says why. Free the port, or change it (Settings).
the voice bot: its packages could not be installedThe machine cannot reach registry.npmjs.org.whip_voice\bin\logs\voicebot-install.log says why. Restart whip_voice to try again.
name is the voice system, so whip_voice is offAnother voice resource started first, and only one can run.Take its ensure out of server.cfg and restart the server.
